incident.title: At approximately 1:03 PM on October 14, 2024 (Turn 2), the R3 Exit Carrier Beam at the Indiana Harbor…
incident.description: At approximately 1:03 PM on October 14, 2024 (Turn 2), the R3 Exit Carrier Beam at the Indiana Harbor 80-inch Hot Strip roughing mill fell from the yoke into the R3 mill pit, landing on the sled and a scaffold platform. No team members were in the pit at the time, though several contractor employees had worked in the pit throughout the morning, and two contractor employees walking beside the mill stand witnessed the fall. The area was red-flagged for investigation. The beam and its link were found intact with the keeper still installed; no damage was apparent on the yoke on which the link rests. A small mill window liner from the top operator side fell with the beam. No crane lifts involving this equipment were in progress or had occurred prior. On the previous shift, the work rolls and top and bottom backup rolls had been removed in preparation for outage work in the mill stand; the R3 top backup roll balance had been left isolated in the raised position, and the B hydraulics had been shut off and bled for work on that system.

starterDocuments.extractedText: R3 carrier beam RCA application test package Page 1SYNTHETIC - TEST USE ONLY SYNTHETIC TEST RECORD - NOT AN ACTUAL COMPANY RECORD Preliminary Incident Notification - Record 16515 A test-ready transcription of the historical preliminary record supplied to the application with the initial incident description. Document ID Incident Record type Status R3-START-001 R3 carrier beam - 10/14/2024 Application test evidence Synthetic / controlled Facility Area Location Event date / shift Indiana Harbor Hot Rolling and Finishing - 80-inch Hot Strip Roughing Mill R3 10/14/2024 - Turn 2 - approximately 1:03 PM Classification Work type Category Potential severity Preliminary contractor case / SIFp Non-routine maintenance Falling object Death Incident description At approximately 1:03 PM on October 14, 2024, the R3 exit carrier beam fell from the yoke into the R3 mill pit, landing on the sled and a scaffold platform. No team members were in the pit at the time. Several contractor employees had worked in the pit during the morning, and two contractor employees walking beside the mill stand witnessed the fall. The area was red-flagged for investigation. The carrier beam and its link were found intact with the keeper still installed. No damage was apparent on the yoke where the link rests. A small mill window liner from the top operator side fell with the beam. No crane lifts involving this equipment were in progress or had occurred prior. On the previous shift, the work rolls and the top and bottom backup rolls had been removed in preparation for outage work in the mill stand. The R3 top backup roll balance had been left isolated in the raised position. The B hydraulics had been shut off and bled for work on that system. Immediate actions Stopped work and red-flagged the area; inspected other mill stands; ensured top roll balances were lowered; verified link-arm keepers were present at other stands; and held a safety stand-down. It is based on developing specific procedures for each space. 1.2 This Confined Space Standard applies to Cleveland-Cliffs Steel personnel and to all contractors who may enter a confined space on Cleveland-Cliffs Steel properties. 1.3 The Take 5 process is an important part of all tasks we perform and whenever possible we shall use this process to minimize the need to enter a confined space. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 3 of 22 Confined Space Safety Standard 2 Responsibilities and Authorities 2.1 This standard was jointly developed with participation from the represented workforce and management. 2.2 Each facility’s management is responsible for the implementation of this standard. 2.3 The Senior Director of Health, Safety and Security is responsible for authorizing this standard. 2.4 Confined Space Entry Procedures must be reviewed and revised as necessary. This must be done: 2.4.1 Annually or before the next entry. 2.4.2 Following any unplanned event. 2.4.3 After any change which may affect the entry. 2.5 It is the responsibility of the department "owning" or controlling the confined space to maintain the Confined Space Entry Procedure, keep canceled permits and keep contractor notification and debriefing records for at least one year. 2.6 The Confined Space Entry Program and entry procedures are subject to annual review and periodic audit to ensure proper program direction and execution. 2.7 Each closed permit will be reviewed by the department and filed in a way that allows review for a period of 1 year. 2.7.1 Each department must review their program annually. Page 4 of 22 Confined Space Safety Standard 3 References and Definitions 3.1 References • 29 CFR 1910.146 • 29 CFR 1926.1200 • MIOSHA-STD-1160 3.2 Definitions Attendant: An individual stationed outside a confined space who monitors the authorized entrants and performs all the attendant's duties assigned in the confined space program. The Attendant will be assigned no other duties that prevent the accomplishment of the duties required. Acceptable Entry Conditions: The conditions that must exist in a permit space to allow entry and to ensure that employees involved with a permit-required confined space entry can safely enter and work within the space. Alternate Entry Procedures: Procedures that may be used when the only hazard of a confined space, based upon monitoring and inspection data, is an actual or potential hazardous atmosphere in which continuous forced air ventilation alone is all that is needed to maintain the Permit Required Confined Space for safe entry. Authorized Entrant: An employee who is authorized by the employer to enter a permit required confined space. Blanking or Blinding: The absolute closure of a pipe, line, or duct by the fastening of a solid plate (such as a spectacle blind or a skillet blind) that completely covers the bore and that can withstand the maximum pressure of the pipe, line or duct with no leakage beyond the plate. Competent Person: One who can identify existing and predictable hazards in the surroundings or working conditions which are unsanitary, hazardous, or dangerous to employees, and who has the authorization to take prompt corrective measures to eliminate them. ∆ Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 5 of 22 Confined Space Safety Standard Confined Space: A space that: • Is large enough and so configured that an employee can bodily enter and perform assigned work. • Has limited or restricted means for entry or exit (for example, tanks, vessels, storage bins, hoppers, vaults, pits, ladles, and sewers that may have limited means of entry). • Is not designed for continuous occupancy. Double Block and Bleed: The closure of a line, duct, or pipe by closing and locking two in-line valves, and by opening and locking a drain or vent valve in the line between the two closed valves. Emergency: Any occurrence (including any failure of hazard control or monitoring equipment) or event(s), internal or external, to the confined space that could endanger entrants. Engulfment: The surrounding and effective capture of a person by a liquid or finely divided (flowable) solid substance that can be aspirated to cause death by filling or plugging the respiratory system, or that can exert enough force on the body to cause death by strangulation, constriction or crushing. Entrant: An employee authorized by the entry supervisor to enter a confined space. Entrapment: The capture and potential asphyxiation of a person by being trapped in a confined space. • With inwardly converging walls. • A floor which slopes downward or tapers to a smaller cross section. Entry: The action by which a person passes through an opening into a confined space. Entry includes ensuing work activities in that space and is considered to have occurred as soon as any part of the entrant's body breaks the plane of an opening into the space. Entry Supervisor: The person responsible for determining if acceptable entry conditions are present at a permit space where entry is planned, for authorizing entry and overseeing entry operations, and for terminating entry. Entry Permit System: The employer's written procedures for preparing and issuing permits for entry and returning the permit space to service following termination of entry and designates by name or title the individuals who may authorize entry. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 6 of 22 Confined Space Safety Standard Entry Permit: The written or printed document that is provided by the employer to allow and control entry into a permit space, and contains the information specified in section 5 of this document. Hazardous Atmosphere: An atmosphere that may expose employees to the risk of death, incapacitation, and impairment of ability to self-rescue (that is, escape unaided from a permit space), injury or acute illness from one or more of the following causes: • Flammable gas, vapor, or mist more than 10 percent of its lower flammable limit (LFL). • Airborne combustible dust at a concentration that meets or exceeds its LFL (dust obscuring vision at 5 feet). • Atmospheric Oxygen concentration below 19.5 percent or above 23.5 percent. • The presence of any substance whose concentration exceeds a recognized permissible exposure limit or dose. For those substances that have no permissible exposure level or dose, refer to other recognized data such as safety data sheets, manufacturers' data, and lab analysis for determining acceptable conditions. • Atmospheric concentration of any substance which may exceed a permissible exposure limit. • Any other atmospheric condition that is immediately dangerous to life or health. Hot Work Permit: The employer's written authorization to perform operations (for example, riveting, welding, cutting, burning, and heating) capable of providing a source of ignition. Immediately Dangerous to Life or Health (IDLH): Any condition that poses an immediate or delayed threat to life, or that would cause irreversible adverse health effects, or that would interfere with an individual's ability to escape unaided from a permit space. Inerting: The displacement of the atmosphere in a permit space by a noncombustible gas (such as nitrogen) to such an extent that the resulting atmosphere is noncombustible. Isolation: The process by which a permit space is removed from service and completely protected against the release of energy and material into the space by such means as: blanking or blinding; misaligning or removing sections of lines, pipes or ducts; a double block and bleed system; lockout of all sources of energy; or blocking or disconnecting all mechanical linkages. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 7 of 22 Confined Space Safety Standard Line Breaking: The intentional opening of a pipe, line or duct that is or has been carrying flammable, corrosive or toxic material, an inert gas, or any fluid at a volume, pressure, or temperature capable of causing injury. Non-Permit Confined Space: A confined space that does not contain, or with respect to atmospheric hazards, have the potential to contain any hazard capable of causing death or serious physical harm. Oxygen Deficient Atmosphere: An atmosphere containing less than 19.5 percent oxygen by volume. Oxygen Enriched Atmosphere: An atmosphere containing more than 23.5 percent oxygen by volume. Permit Required Confined Space: Means a confined space that has one or more of the following characteristics: • Contains or has the potential to contain a hazardous atmosphere. • Contains material that has the potential for engulfment of an entrant. • Has an internal configuration such that an entrant could be trapped or asphyxiated by inwardly converging walls, or a floor which slopes downward and tapers to a smaller cross-section or; • Contains any other recognized serious safety or health hazard. PEL (Permission Exposure Limit): Average concentration that must not be exceeded during an 8-hour work shift of a 40-hour work week. Permit System: The employer's written procedure for preparing and issuing permits for entry, and for returning the permit space to service following termination of entry. Permit Required Confined Space Program: The employer's overall program for controlling, and where appropriate, for protecting employees from permit space hazards and for regulating employee entry into permit spaces. Prohibited Condition: Any condition in a permit space that is not allowed by the permit during the period when entry is authorized. Qualified Person: One who, by possession of a recognized degree, certificate, or professional standing, or who by extensive knowledge, training, and experience, has successfully demonstrated his ability to solve or resolve problems relating to the subject matter, the work or the project. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 8 of 22 Confined Space Safety Standard Retrieval System: The equipment (including a retrieval line, full body harness, wristlets, if appropriate, and a lifting device or anchor) used for non-entry rescue of persons from the permit space. Representative Permit Space: A mock-up of a confined space that has entrance openings that are similar to, and is of similar size, configuration, and accessibility to the permit space that authorized entrants enter. Rescue Service: The personnel designated to rescue employees from permit spaces. • Rescue services need to be qualified and selected to perform rescue services. • Cleveland-Cliffs Steel Safety will determine what contractors are qualified to perform rescue services. Testing: The process by which the hazards that may confront entrants of a permit space are identified and evaluated. Testing includes specifying the tests that are to be performed in the permit space. Testing enables employers both to devise and implement adequate control measures for the protection of authorized entrants and to determine if acceptable entry conditions are present immediately prior to, and during entry. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 10 of 22 Confined Space Safety Standard 5 Requirements 5.1 General Responsibilities 5.1.1 Divisions/Departments are responsible for: a. Identifying all confined spaces in their areas. b. Identifying and post signage and maintain signage at all confined spaces. c. Maintain an inventory of all confined spaces. d. Ensuring all personnel who enter confined spaces are trained. e. Implementing this confined space entry program. f. Performing confined space hazard assessments. g. Developing space specific entry procedure. h. Ensure all spaces are maintained closed to prevent unauthorized access. i. Maintain the space so that a tool or the removal of latches or similar methods is needed to gain entry. j. Ensuring that contractor requirements of this program are implemented. k. Ensuring that all contractors who may enter a confined space are made aware of this program. 5.1.2 Health and Safety Department is responsible for: a. Assisting departments in identifying confined spaces. b. Assisting departments in completion of required training. c. Assisting departments with confined space assessments. d. Assisting departments in monitoring people working in confined spaces. e. Auditing the program. Printed Copy is for reference only. Adopting the Cleveland-Cliffs confined space program or implementing one that meets or exceeds the Cleveland-Cliffs program. b. Training their employees. c. Supplying their own safety and monitoring equipment. d. Maintaining the permit used for entry. 5.1.4 Entry Alternatives a. When work is assigned, the crew should utilize the Take 5 process to identify if entry into the space will be required. b. Whenever feasible, design changes or work practice will be developed to eliminate the need for entry into confined spaces. c. Non-entry work practices will be covered by a JSA or equivalent methods of standardized work instruction. 5.2 Confined Space 5.2.1 For Cleveland-Cliffs, all locations that meet all the following criteria are to be considered as a CONFINED SPACE: a. Is large enough and so configured that an employee can bodily enter and perform assigned work and, b. Has limited or restricted means for entry or exit (for example, tanks, vessels, storage bins, hoppers, vaults, pits, sewers and roll off containers that may have limited means of entry), c. Is not designed for continuous occupancy. 5.2.2 Permit Required Confined spaces contain at least one of the following: a. Contains, or has the potential to contain, a hazardous atmosphere. b. Contains, or has the potential to contain, flowable material that could engulf. c. Has an internal configuration such that one could be trapped or asphyxiated by an inwardly converging wall or by a floor which slopes downward and tapers to a small cross section. d. Contains any other recognized serious safety or health hazard. (An example of this situation would be exposed, uninsulated electrical wiring.) Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 12 of 22 Confined Space Safety Standard 5.2.3 Cleveland-Cliffs requires all confined space entry to utilize an entry permit and be attended as if it were a permitted space. Spaces that meet the definition of a Permit Required space also require rescue services. 5.3 Confined Space Inventory 5.3.1 A complete inventory of all known confined spaces within a department will be made and reviewed annually. Additional spaces will be included upon discovery. It is the responsibility of the department to generate this inventory and keep it current. 5.3.2 This inventory shall be reviewed annually or more frequently as necessary to maintain an accurate inventory. 5.3.3 Made accessible to all employees as needed. 5.3.4 The inventory will uniquely identify each space. a. Department, Unique number, Common Name. Example: Rolling Mill (Space) 29 Pit pumps (RM-29- Pit Pumps) 5.4 Posting 5.4.1 All Employees must be alerted to the presence of the confined space. 5.4.2 Appropriate actions must be taken to prevent unauthorized entry. 5.4.3 All accessible entrances to inventoried confined spaces shall be posted near the entrance with the following: DANGER: CONFINED SPACE AUTHORIZED ENTRY ONLY (or similar language to identify spaces at each facility in a consistent manner.) 5.4.4 All spaces including manholes in roadways will be uniquely identified. 5.4.5 A unique identifier will be posted at each space near the point of entry. 5.4.6 If you discover an area that might be a confined space and it is not marked as such, notify your supervisor. 5.5 Entry Procedures 5.5.1 Safe entry procedures for confined spaces must be developed and written in a standard step-by-step format. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 13 of 22 Confined Space Safety Standard 5.5.2 These step-by-step procedures must be created with enough detail and supporting documentation, such as pictures and diagrams, that a person preparing to enter a confined space can verify that the actions required, and conditions specified do exist and that the actions required have been met. 5.5.3 It is the responsibility of the department controlling the confined space to create, maintain, review, revise and approve the entry procedure. 5.5.4 Approval of new and revised entry procedures must be approved by the Operating Department Division Manager or Section Manager, Maintenance Section Manager., and the Safety Department. a. Confined spaces entered at least once a year must have specific entry procedures, pre-planned and in writing. Whenever possible these must be created in advance of any entry to allow thorough review by operations, maintenance, safety, and entry groups. b. Spaces entered less frequently than once per year shall have their procedures developed prior to entry as soon as the need to enter the space is recognized. 5.5.5 Current copies of any referenced documents must be attached to the Confined Space Permit at the time of use. a. Includes SDS for materials that may already be present in the space, and for materials that entrants might introduce into the space. SDS (Safety Data Sheet) information must be reviewed to assure all hazards are eliminated or controlled. b. Includes energy control procedures. c. Includes hot work permits if necessary. d. For contractors includes Joint Job Hazard Assessment and Controls form 5.6 Confined Space Permit 5.6.1 Confined Space Permit is to be used as written documentation to assure that all hazards or potential hazards are dealt with appropriately. 5.6.2 The Confined Space Permit is the working document completed to gain and maintain an entry into a space. 5.6.3 Until the Confined Space Permit is completed, the Confined Space shall be considered to contain a hazard. ∆ Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 14 of 22 Confined Space Safety Standard 5.6.4 Confined Space Entry Permits do not include or take the place of hot work permits. 5.6.5 The Confined Space Entry Permit must contain the following information: a. The date and time of entry. b. The expiration time of the entry. c. The name and location of the permit space. d. The purpose of the entry. e. The hazards of the permit space to be entered and the acceptable entry conditions. f. The identity of each authorized entrant, each attendant, and the entry supervisor. g. The measures to be taken to isolate the permit space and to eliminate or control permit space hazards before entry. h. The results of initial and periodic tests performed with the identity of testers. i. The name and telephone numbers of rescue and emergency services and means to be used to contact them. j. The additional permits, such as for hot work, have been issued authorizing work in the permit space. k. Special equipment and procedures, including PPE (Personal Protective Equipment) and alarm systems. 5.6.6 Confined space permits will expire after 12 hours and must be re- issued. 5.7 Attendant 5.7.1 An attendant is required for any entry into any confined space. 5.7.2 Under no circumstances will the confined space Attendant enter the confined space. 5.8 Entry Supervisor 5.8.1 An entry supervisor is required for every confined space. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 15 of 22 Confined Space Safety Standard 5.9 Rescue 5.9.1 Rescue Standards: a. If hazards within a confined space cannot be eliminated, and if rescue cannot be done from outside the space, or the conditions in the space are Immediately Dangerous to Life and Health (IDLH), a rescue team is required. b. If rescue is provided by a non-Cleveland-Cliffs source, advanced access to the confined space and training on associated hazards must be provided. c. Confined spaces that require rescue teams must have the rescue team and required equipment on-site and within range of the space as pre-determined prior to entry. They must also be in range of the emergency signal or method of summoning the rescue team. d. A rescue team may be utilized for more than one space and does not need to be staged at the entry unless the conditions of entry require one to be immediately available. 5.9.2 Rescue from outside the confined space. a. If it is determined that rescue can be performed from outside the confined space, the person(s) responsible for rescue must be trained in the following: b. Use of the mechanical hoist or other equipment that will be used to retrieve the entrant. c. Any hazards that exist outside of the confined space that could interfere with rescue. d. The necessary emergency numbers and how to access communications. e. Rescue personnel must be provided with quick access to communications equipment so that emergency personnel can be contacted immediately if rescue operations are put into effect. 5.9.3 Non-entry rescue equipment and setup. a. Non-Entry Rescue equipment to be used by trained personnel includes items such as but not limited to a tripod, davit arm and horizontal retrieval device with approved retrieval systems. b. Full body harnesses are to be worn by all entrants going into a confined space when needed to facilitate rescue. ∆ Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 16 of 22 Confined Space Safety Standard c. A tripod or similar rescue device will be positioned to the side of vertical confined spaces and checked for stability prior to entry by the attendee and individuals working in the confined space. Once opened, the tripod will be placed over the vertical opening to assure stability and fit for rescue. After checking the tripod, it can be situated to the side of the confined space opening. d. All atmospheric testing and ventilation shall be conducted according to the established confined space program and be posted at/or near the opening of the space. e. Under no circumstances will a crane or powered hoist be used in a rescue operation. 5.10 Duties of Confined Space Participants 5.10.1 Entry team duties. 5.10.2 Duties of authorized entrants: a. Follow entry requirements of the permit. b. Know the hazards that may be faced during entry. c. Wear full body harness when entering the space when needed to facilitate rescue. d. Recognize the signs and symptoms of hazard exposure. e. Understand the consequences of hazardous exposure. f. Use equipment properly. g. Communicate with the attendant. h. Alert the attendant of hazards. i. Exit the permit space immediately when required. j. Wear a personal Four Gas monitor. 5.10.3 Duties of the attendant: a. Know entry hazards. b. Know behavioral effects of exposure to the hazards likely to be present. c. Maintain accurate entrant identification. d. Maintain accurate records on the confined space permit. ∆ Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 17 of 22 Confined Space Safety Standard e. Remain outside the permit space. f. Do not leave the space entry until all Entrants are out of the space or you are relieved by another qualified attendant. g. Communicate with entrants. h. Monitor entry activities. i. Recording readings of the space as required. j. Summon rescue and emergency services. k. Prevent unauthorized entry. l. Perform non-entry rescue. m. Perform no additional duties. n. Remain alert and attentive to the space without distraction. 5.10.4 Duties of the Entry Supervisor: a. Know the potential hazards during entry and work. b. Determine if acceptable entry conditions are present at a permit space where entry is planned. c. Terminate entry as required by the standard. d. Verify that rescue services are readily available and the means for summoning them are operable. e. Remove unauthorized individuals who enter or try to enter the permit space during entry and work. f. Determine that entry and work operations remain consistent with entry permit terms and that acceptable entry conditions are maintained. g. The entry supervisor authorizing the entry may serve as an attendant for the entry. 5.11 Training 5.11.1 Procedures and duties will be reviewed with all affected employees prior to confined space entry. 5.11.2 Training will be conducted before the employee is first assigned duties. 5.11.3 Before a change in assigned duties. ∆ Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 18 of 22 Confined Space Safety Standard 5.11.4 When a change in permit space operations. 5.11.5 Where there are deviations from the permit entry space procedures. 5.11.6 Where inadequacies in employee knowledge occur. 5.11.7 Training in job duties and the proper use of needed equipment, such as air monitoring equipment, will be given and proficiency established prior to entry and or on an annual basis. 5.11.8 Anyone who could serve as an attendant is also to be trained to use non-entry rescue equipment. 5.11.9 If rescue is to be done by a rescue team that will enter the space, they will receive: a. Training as required for equipment such as self-contained breathing apparatus and testing devices. b. Confined space hazard training the same as those entering the space. c. Annual rescue training includes both actual confined spaces and appropriate simulated representative confined spaces. d. Rescue team members will be trained in First aid and Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR). e. A copy of the training will include the materials and topics covered in the training. 5.11.10 Training must be documented as either initial or refresher and maintained for the period that all other training records are maintained (both immediately accessible or via archives) per each business unit’s practice. 5.12 Permission to Enter 5.12.1 No person is allowed to enter a confined space without permission. 5.12.2 No person is allowed to enter a confined space without a calibrated, functioning, personal four gas monitor that monitors O2, LEL, H2S, CO. 5.12.3 Entry means the point at which any part of a person's body breaks the plane into the opening of the space. 5.12.4 A copy of the complete Confined Space Permit, with attachments, must be posted or otherwise made highly visible at the entrance to a confined space before permission to enter is given. ∆ Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 19 of 22 Confined Space Safety Standard 5.12.5 The Entry supervisor for a confined space must grant permission for entry by verifying required entry conditions and signing the permit. 5.12.6 Permission to enter a space can only be given after all aspects of the written entry permit, including attachments, have been met or completed and employees have completed training. 5.13 Canceling an Entry Permit 5.13.1 Permission to enter a confined space is canceled when: a. The task for which the permit was issued has been completed. b. A condition not allowed under the permit arises in or near the space. Any such problems or conditions and their resolution will be noted on the entry permit. c. The permit time limit has expired. 5.14 Monitoring 5.14.1 The level of air contaminants allowed will be evaluated by the Safety Department. This requirement is removed from the Standard. 5.14.2 Initial monitoring or atmospheric testing will be performed from outside the confined space prior to entry. 5.14.3 Initial Atmospheric Assessment will be completed prior to entry and completed from outside the space. 5.14.4 The air monitoring must be representative of the entire confined space including monitoring at the top, middle and bottom of the space to detect any stratification of the gases. 5.14.5 When a draw tube is used adequate time must be used at each level to allow the atmosphere to be drawn through the tube and into the monitor. 5.14.6 Oxygen (O2), Lower Explosive Limit (LEL), and Carbon Monoxide (CO) levels and H2S must be tested in ALL confined space entries at Cleveland-Cliffs. a. O2 (Oxygen) shall be between 19.5% and 23.5%. b. LEL (Lower Explosive Limit) will be less than 5%. c. CO (Carbon Monoxide) will be no greater than 35 PPM. d. H2S (Hydrogen Sulfide) will be no greater than 10 PPM. ∆ Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 20 of 22 Confined Space Safety Standard 5.14.7 Monitoring must also be performed on any other hazard that may be present in the space. 5.14.8 Examples: HCN, Temperature, Ammonia, Radiation 5.14.9 Continuous Monitoring a. The attendant shall at intervals of no greater than 15 minutes monitor the space for changes in acceptable conditions. b. Communication will be established with each entrant based on the permissions to enter. c. Measure the atmosphere using a calibrated 4 gas monitor. d. Monitor for other hazards identified within the space. e. This will be recorded on the entry permit. 5.14.10 All entry operations shall be prohibited when any atmospheric level exceeds Cleveland-Cliffs requirements (<19.5% Oxygen, >23.5% Oxygen, 5% LEL, 35 PPM Carbon Monoxide, 10 PPM H2S). 5.14.11 All entry operations shall be ceased when any atmospheric level exceeds Cleveland-Cliffs requirements (<19.5% Oxygen, >23.5% Oxygen, 5% LEL, 35 PPM Carbon Monoxide, 10 PPM H2S). 5.14.12 Unless an alternative protective measure such as supplied air was determined to be required as a condition of entry. 5.14.13 Under special conditions for entry the conditions that prohibit the continued operation will be specified on the permit. 5.14.14 Results of the monitoring must be immediately provided to each entrant. 5.14.15 Each entrant must be provided with the opportunity to observe the pre- entry and any subsequent monitoring of the confined space. 5.15 Contractors 5.15.1 All contractors that take part in any aspect of confined space entry operations must, at a minimum, follow Cleveland-Cliffs Steel Confined Space Entry Procedures. Contractors must follow all Cleveland-Cliffs Steel documentation requirements involving Confined Space Entry Procedures. ∆ Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 21 of 22 Confined Space Safety Standard 5.15.2 The Cleveland-Cliffs Steel person responsible for bringing the contractor on site must notify the contractor about hazards of the confined space, Cleveland-Cliffs Steel monitoring requirements and Cleveland-Cliffs Steel Confined Space Entry Procedures. This notification must be documented. 5.15.3 The Cleveland-Cliffs Steel person responsible for bringing the contractor on site must ensure that the required debriefing is completed at the conclusion of the confined space entry. 5.15.4 Contractors shall provide their own monitors with proper calibration and a current bump test prior to the issue of a confined space permit. 6 Forms and Documented Information 6.1 Attachments / Forms 6.1.1 Confined Space Assessment Form Template (CCS-HSS-FRM-012.2) 6.1.2 Confined Space Permit Template (CCS-HSS-FRM-011.2) 7 Opportunities and Risks 7.1 This Standard is to ensure a consistent approach to confined space programs are used at all Cleveland-Cliffs Steelmaking facilities. 7.2 The Standard addresses: 7.2.1 Risk reduction. 7.2.2 Improved entry conditions. 7.2.3 Achieves desired conditions for entry. 7.2.4 Requires continued improvement. Page 2 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard 1 Purpose/Scope 1.1 Establish minimum standards for all Cleveland-Cliffs Steel Operations to protect employees and contracted workers that are exposed to potential falls greater than 4 feet or working above dangerous equipment. In addition, it establishes the scope, training, and use of fall protection systems by Cleveland-Cliffs Steel employees in Cleveland-Cliffs Steel facilities. 1.2 This standard shall establish a means to analyze elevated work tasks, determine appropriate controls and protect personnel from fall to below hazards. Page 6 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard 3.2 Definitions Anchorage or Anchorage Point: A secure point of attachment for lifelines, lanyards, or deceleration devices capable of supporting 5,000 pounds per person or is designed by a qualified person and are a part of a complete fall protection system maintaining a safety factor of at least two. Arresting Force: The force generated by arresting the test weight that is transmitted through the fall arresting system components to the anchorage or load cell. Authorized Person: A person approved or assigned to perform a specific type of duty or duties or to be at a specific location or job site (e.g., building maintenance, roof repair, etc.). Employees who are required to wear fall protection during work activities. Body Harness: A design of straps which may be secured about the employee in a manner that will distribute the fall arrest forces over at least the thighs, pelvis, waist, chest, and shoulders with means for attaching it to other components of a personal fall arrest system. Competent Person: A person who is capable of identifying existing and predictable hazards in any personal fall protection system or any component of it, as well as in their application and uses with related equipment, and who has authorization to take prompt, corrective action to eliminate the identified hazards. Cage/Basket Guard: An enclosure that is fastened to the side rails of the fixed ladder or to the structure to encircle the climbing space of the ladder for the safety of the person who must climb the ladder. Connector: A device used to couple (connect) parts of the personal fall arrest system together. Carabiner: A connector component comprised of a trapezoidal or oval-shaped body with a normally closed gate. The gate, when released, automatically closes to retain the object. All carabiners used in fall protection systems must be the automatic locking type and have a minimum tensile strength of 5,000 pounds (22 kN). Dangerous Equipment: Equipment (such as pickling or galvanizing tanks, degreasing units, machinery, electrical equipment, and other units) which, as a result of form or function, may be hazardous to employees who fall onto or into such equipment. Deceleration Device: Any mechanism which serves to lessen the arresting force on the body during a fall. Deceleration Distance: The vertical distance a falling employee travels from the point at which the deceleration device begins to operate, excluding lifeline elongation and free fall distance, until stopping. It is measured as the distance between the location of an employee's body harness attachment point at the moment of activation (at the onset of fall arrest forces) of the deceleration device during a fall, and the location of that attachment point after the employee comes to a full stop. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 7 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard Fall Arrest System: A system that prevents a worker from falling and contacting a lower level. It consists of an anchorage, connectors, a full body harness, and may include a lanyard, deceleration device, lifeline, or any combination of the before-mentioned items. Fall Clearance Calculation: The total calculated distance required to prevent workers from hitting the ground or lower level, in case of a fall. Free Fall: The act of falling before a personal fall arrest system begins to apply force to arrest the fall. Free Fall Distance: The vertical displacement of the fall arrest attachment point on the employee's body harness between the onset of the fall and just before the system begins to apply force to arrest the fall. This distance excludes deceleration distance, and lifeline/lanyard elongation, but includes any deceleration device slide distance or self-retracting lifeline/lanyard extension before they operate and fall arrest forces occur. (Always minimize Free Fall Distance not to exceed 6 feet.) Fixed Ladder: A ladder which is permanently attached to a structure, building or equipment. (Does not include ship stairs, step bolts or manhole steps.) All new or modified fixed ladders greater than 24 feet shall have a ladder safety system or fall arrest system. Existing fixed ladders must have a ladder safety system or fall arrest system by November 2036. Guardrail System: A barrier erected along an unprotected or exposed side, edge, or other areas of a walking/working surface to prevent workers from falling to a lower level. The system consists of a top rail at 42 inches (plus or minus three inches) above the walking surface, a midrail at a height midway between the top edge of the guardrail and the walking surface. A toe board is required to ensure falling object protection along the exposed edge of overhead walking/working surfaces sufficient to protect employees below. Handrail System: A barrier erected to prevent employees from falling to lower levels. Handrails are not less than 30 inches and not more than 38 inches measured from the edge of the stair tread. There must be a minimum of 2.5 inches clearance between the handrail and any other object. Lanyard: A flexible line of rope, cable, or strap with self-locking snap hook connectors at each end for connecting to body harnesses or deceleration devices. Ladder Safety System: A system (usually consisting of a carrier, safety sleeve, lanyard, connectors, and body harness) attached to a fixed ladder designed to eliminate or reduce the possibility of a worker falling from the ladder. Leading Edge: The edge of a floor, roof or other walking/working surface which changes location as additional floor, roof, etc., is placed or constructed. A leading edge is considered an unprotected side or edge. Lifeline: A component consisting of a flexible line for connection to an anchorage at one end to hang vertically (vertical lifelines), or for connection to anchorages at both ends to stretch horizontally (horizontal lifeline), and which serves as a means for connecting other components of a personal fall arrest system to the anchorage. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 8 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard Low-Slope Roof: A roof having a slope less than or equal to 4 in 12 (vertical to horizontal). Personal Fall Arrest System: System used to arrest an employee in a fall from a working level. It consists of an anchorage, connectors, full body harness and a self-retractable lifeline/lanyard. Personal Fall Protection: A system that is used to arrest an employee in a fall from a working level. The fall protection must consist of a full body harness, a lanyard with a deceleration device and an anchorage or lifeline with approved hooking devices as specified in Cleveland- Cliffs Fall Protection Standard. Qualified Person: One who, by possession of a recognized degree, certificate, or professional standing, or who by extensive knowledge, training and experience, has successfully demonstrated ability to solve or resolve problems relating to the subject matter, the work or the project. Rope Grab: A cam-type deceleration device that travels on a lifeline and automatically engages the lifeline and locks to arrest an employee’s fall. Safety Factor: An added margin of security against risk. Safety Net Systems: A horizontal or semi-horizontal, cantilever-style barrier that uses a netting system to stop falling workers before they contact a lower level or obstruction. Safety Monitor: A competent person responsible for recognizing and warning workers of fall hazards. Self-Retracting Lifeline/Lanyard: Deceleration device containing a drum-wound line which can be slowly extracted from, or retracted onto, the drum under slight tension during normal employee movement, and which after the onset of a fall, automatically locks the drum and arrests the fall. Steep Roof: Roof having slope of greater than 4 in 12 (vertical to horizontal). Snap Hook: A connector comprised of a hook-shaped member with a closed keeper, which may be opened to permit the hook to receive an object, and when released, automatically closes to retain the object. Snap hooks must be self-closing with a self-locking keeper, which remains closed and locked until unlocked and pressed open for connection or disconnection, thus preventing the opportunity for the object to “roll out” of the snap hook. Snap hooks used for fall protection systems must have a 3,600-pound gate strength. Swing Fall: The potential for a worker using a personal fall arrest system to fall and swing in a pendulum motion, subjecting the worker to strike a fixed object or other hazards. This can occur if a worker falls and the anchorage is not directly overhead, and a fall allows the worker to swing toward the anchor point. Tie Off: The act of a person wearing personal fall protection equipment, connecting directly to an anchorage point. 100 % tie off is required when exposed to a fall hazard while using Travel Restraint or Fall Arrest systems. Page 9 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard Toe Board: A solid horizontal guard installed along the exposed edge of overhead walking/working surfaces to prevent the fall of materials and equipment to lower levels and protect employees below. They must be a minimum of 3.5 inches and not have an opening more than 0.25 inches above the walking/working surface. Total Fall Distance: Adding the free fall distance, lanyard deceleration distance depending on the equipment (24” for ANSI Z359.14-2014 Class A, 54” for ANSI Z359.14-2014 Class B, 42” for ANSI Z359.14-2021 Class 1 and Class 2), harness stretch, the distance your body extended from the dorsal ring of your harness attached to your anchorage point, and a 3-foot safety factor. Trauma Straps: A pair of straps attached to a full body harness that allows a worker, who is suspended, to stand up in their harness and to relieve the pressure being applied to the arteries and veins around the top of the legs. Travel Restraint (Tether) Line: A rope or wire rope used to transfer forces from a body support to an anchorage or anchorage connector in a travel restraint system. Travel Restraint System: A combination of an anchorage, anchorage connector, lanyard (or other means of connection) and body support intended to be used by an employee to limit travel to prevent exposure to a fall hazard. A travel restraint system is used such that it does not support any portion of the employee's weight; otherwise, the system would be a positioning system or a personal fall arrest system. Travel restraint lines must be capable of sustaining a tensile load of at least 5,000 pounds (22.2 kN). Unprotected Sides or Edges: Any side or edge (except at entrances to points of access) of a walking/working surface; e.g., floor, roof, ramp, or runway where there is no wall or guardrail system at least 39 inches high. Walking/Working Surface: Any surface, whether horizontal or vertical, on which an employee walks or works, including but not limited to floors, roofs, ramps, bridges, runways, framework, and concrete reinforcing steel. Work Positioning: A system consisting of a body harness, lanyards, and anchorage devices rigged to allow a person to be supported on an elevated vertical surface, such as a wall or fixed ladder, and work with both hands free. Attachments should be at the workers hips as preferred method while using a work positioning system. ∆ Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 21 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard 5.6.3.6 Buckle tongues must be free of distortion in shape and motion. They must overlap buckle frames and move freely back and forth in their socket. The roller must turn freely on the frame. Check for distortion or sharp edges. 5.6.3.7 Trauma straps must be present and not damaged. 5.6.3.8 Any additional inspection procedures required by the equipment manufacturer as provided in training. 5.6.4 Lanyard Inspection. 5.6.4.1 Travel Restraint Lanyard Inspection: When inspecting lanyards, begin at one end and work to the opposite end. Slowly rotate the lanyard so that the entire circumference is checked. Stitched (spliced) ends require extra attention. 5.6.4.2 The double locking snaps will be inspected closely for hook and eye distortions, cracks, corrosion, or pitted surfaces. The keeper (latch) must seat into the nose without binding and not be distorted or obstructed. The keeper spring will exert sufficient force to firmly close the keeper. Keeper locks must prevent the keeper from opening when the keeper closes. 5.6.4.3 The thimble must be firmly seated in the eye of the splice, and the splice must have no loose or cut strands. In addition, the edges of the thimble must be free of sharp edges, distortions, or cracks. 5.6.4.4 While bending a web lanyard over a pipe or mandrel, observe each side of the webbing. This will reveal any cuts or breaks, swelling, discoloration, cracks, charring or obvious signs of chemical or heat damage. 5.6.4.5 Rotation of the rope lanyard while inspecting from end to end will reveal any fuzzy, worn, broken, or cut fibers. Weakened areas from extreme loads will appear as a noticeable change in original diameter. The rope diameter must be uniform throughout, following a short break-in period. 5.6.4.6 Any additional inspection procedures required by the equipment manufacturer as provided in training. 5.6.5 Snap hooks (including carabineers). 5.6.5.1 Snap hooks must be of the locking type designed and used to prevent disengagement of the snap hook by the contact of the snap hook keeper by the connected member. Snap hooks must be proof tested by the manufacturer to a minimum tensile load of 3,600 pounds, (normal 5,000 pounds) without cracking, breaking, or taking permanent deformation. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 22 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard 5.6.5.2 The keeper of the snap hook must have a spring tension that will not allow the keeper to open with a weight of 25 pounds or less, but the keeper must begin to open with a weight of 4 pounds supported on the keeper against the end of the nose. 5.6.5.3 Inspection of the snap hook must include: • Signs of cracking. • Sharp edges. • Signs of breaking. • Permanent deformation. • Pitted or corroded surfaces. • Keeper must seat properly without binding or obstruction. • Keeper spring must exert sufficient force to ensure closure. • Locks must prevent keeper from opening. 5.6.6 Inspection of Retractable Lanyards: • Anchorage connectors shall be checked for bent, cracked, or distorted components. • With the device in the mounted position, test the lanyard retraction and tension by pulling out several feet of the lanyard and allowing it to retract back into the unit. Always maintain a light tension on the lanyard as it retracts. The lanyard should pull out freely and retract all the way back into the unit. a. If the lanyard does not pull out smoothly or sticks when retracting, pull the entire lanyard out of the housing and allow it to retract slowly under tension. b. The lanyard must be checked for signs of damage. Inspect for cuts, burns, corrosion, kinks, frays or worn areas. Inspect any sewing for loose, broken, or damaged stitches. • The braking mechanism shall be tested by grasping the lifeline above the impact indicator (if equipped) and applying a sharp, steady pull downward which will engage the brakes. There should be no slippage of the lifeline while the brakes are engaged. Once tension is released, the brakes will disengage, and the unit will return to the retractable mode. • Check the snap hook to ensure that it operates freely and locks. Inspect the snap hook for any signs of damage to the keepers and any bent, cracked, or distorted components. • Load indicators, if equipped, will typically be located above the snap hook. An indicator will be exposed when subjected to fall arresting forces. Check manufacturer instructions for indicator type and location. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 23 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard • Any additional inspection procedures required by the equipment manufacturer shall be observed. 5.6.7 Visual Indications of Damage to Webbing and Lanyards: 5.6.7.1 Nylon & Cordura: • Heat Damage – In excessive heat, nylon becomes brittle and has a shriveled brownish appearance. In addition, fibers will break when flexed. Therefore, nylon must never be used above 200 degrees Fahrenheit. Refer to limitations listed in the manufacturer’s user manual. • Chemical Damage – Color change usually appears as a brownish smear or smudge. Transverse cracks when harness or lanyard is bent over a pipe. There will also be a loss of elasticity in the harness or lanyard. • Flame/Molten Metal Damage – Webbing strands fuse together. Hard, shiny spots and brittle feel but will not support combustion. • Paint/Solvent Damage – Paint, which penetrates and dries, restricts the movement of fibers. Drying agents and solvents in some paints will appear as chemical damage. 5.6.7.2 Polyester & Dacron: • Heat Damage – Same as nylon above, except do not use above 180 degrees Fahrenheit. Refer to limitations listed in the manufacturer’s user manual. • Chemical Damage – Same as nylon above. • Flame/Molten Metal Damage – Same as nylon above, except will support combustion. • Paint/Solvent Damage – Same as nylon above. 5.6.7.3 Cable: • Slightly bend and rotate the cable. • Visually check for damaged, kinked, broken strands or unusual discoloration or wear patterns. 5.7 Cleaning and Storage of Fall Protection Equipment 5.7.1 Cleaning: Wipe off all surface dirt with a sponge dampened in plain water. Squeeze the sponge dry. Dip the sponge in a mild solution of water and commercial soap or detergent. Work up a thick lather with vigorous back and forth motions. Wipe the belt dry with a clean cloth. Equipment shall hang freely to dry thoroughly without close exposure to heat, steam, or prolonged periods of sunlight. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 24 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard 5.7.2 Never use chemical cleaners such as naphtha, turpentine, acetone, or other similar products. Never use bleach, rubbing alcohol, hydrogen peroxide or other products with sanitizing or disinfecting claims. The effect of these substances on equipment has not been evaluated and may compromise material integrity. 5.7.3 Storage: Never store personal fall arrest equipment on the ground or outdoors exposed to the elements (e.g., sun, rain, snow), or in an area with exposure to harmful substances or corrosive elements. 5.7.4 Refer to the manufacturer’s recommendations for additional cleaning and storage considerations. 5.8 Training 5.8.1 Each employee authorized to wear fall protection equipment shall be trained to recognize the hazards of falling, and procedures to be followed to minimize these hazards. The employee shall be trained by a person who is competent in the following areas: • Nature of fall hazards in the work area and how to recognize them. • The correct procedures for installing, inspecting, operating, maintaining, and disassembling the personal fall protection systems. • The correct use of personal fall protection systems and equipment including, but not limited to, proper hook-up, anchoring and tie-off techniques, and methods of equipment inspection and storage, as specified by the manufacturer. • The use and operation of guardrail systems, personal fall arrest systems and other protection to be used. • Limitations of fall protection system including proper hook-up, anchoring and tie-off techniques. • Requirements set forth in this program and the procedures to be followed to minimize fall hazards. • Emergency and Rescue procedures. 5.8.2 Content of Fall Protection Training • OSHA’s requirements for fall protection. • Contents of Cleveland-Cliffs Steel Fall Protection Standard. • Basic skills in fall hazard recognition and control. • Donning and Doffing. • Proper methods of inspecting personal fall protection equipment. • Fall Clearance Calculation methods. • Fall protection systems used at Cleveland-Cliffs Steel. • Hazards associated with fall protection. • Rescue and retrieval requirements. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 25 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard 5.8.3 Training must occur initially before exposure, annually, and when there are changes in the types of fall protection systems or equipment or there are changes in the workplace that render previous training obsolete. 5.8.4 The employee shall be retrained when there is reason to believe the employee does not have the understanding and skill required to follow this procedure. A competent person must conduct any required retraining. 5.8.5 The training shall be documented with the name of the employee, identification number, the date(s) of training and the signature of the person conducting the training. 5.8.6 After the completing the training, a documented quiz or test must be administered to ensure that the employee has acquired the understanding, knowledge and skills necessary to safely perform their duties. 5.9 Safety Net Systems 5.9.1 Safety Net Systems can be used when no other fall protection system is available. Safety Nets must be designed and tested by a qualified person and inspected by a competent person. 5.9.2 A safety net system can be erected in a vertical or horizontal plane or both. It must protect the worker from free falling to a lower level or structure. In addition, it must protect employees from falling tools or debris from the worksite. 5.9.3 Safety nets must be installed as close to the area as possible and must never be more than 30 feet below the highest working surface from which a person may fall. 5.9.4 Nets must be hung with sufficient clearance under them to prevent contact with the surface or structures below when subjected to an impact force equal to the drop test specified by OSHA. 5.9.5 Safety nets and safety net installations must be drop tested at the job site after initial installation before using as a fall protection system, whenever relocated, after major repair, and at six-month intervals, if left in one place. 5.9.6 If it can be demonstrated that it is unreasonable to perform the drop test, a competent person must certify the net and that the net installation is in compliance. 5.9.7 The mesh size of nets must not exceed 6 inches by 6 inches. All new nets must meet accepted performance standards of minimum impact resistance as determined and certified by the manufacturer and must bear a label of proof testing. Border ropes must provide a minimum breaking strength of 5,000 pounds. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 26 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard 5.9.8 Safety nets must not extend outward from the outermost projection of the work surface as described by the OSHA table. Forged steel safety hooks or shackles must be used to fasten the net to its supports. Connections between net panels must develop the full strength of the net. 5.9.9 Net systems must be checked and documented daily and cleaned whenever debris is in the net. Remove any damaged nets for repair or replacement. When nets are removed, no work must take place in that area unless another fall protection system is used. Spare nets may be installed to replace damaged nets if all other components pass an inspection, and a competent person checks the new net. 5.10 Rescue 5.10.1 Emergency and rescue procedures must be developed for rescuing a worker within 10 minutes who has fallen from elevated heights. 5.10.2 An Emergency and Rescue Plan must be developed by the operating department in coordination with the Recue Team. It must include an effective rescue summoning method. It must be in place and discussed prior to any Personal Fall Protection System use. 5.10.3 Emergency teams must be trained on the procedure. 5.11 Investigation of a Fall 5.11.1 All employees involved in a fall arrest or fall must be sent immediately for a medical evaluation to determine the extent of injuries. 5.11.2 All falls must be investigated following Cleveland-Cliffs Steel incident investigation procedures. A competent person in fall protection must attend the investigation as a resource. 5.11.3 Once exposed to a fall, remove fall protection equipment from service immediately and destroy when required after analysis and review by representatives from the Safety and Engineering Departments. Remove the destroyed equipment from any inventory list. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 27 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard 6 Forms and Documented Information 6.1 All training must be documented. 6.2 All investigations must be documented in the appropriate Cleveland- Cliffs Steel investigation format. 6.3 Certified anchorage points and lifelines (engineered systems) in buildings, on roofs and external working places where appropriate must be inventoried, inspected and documented. 6.4 Annual inspection of personal fall protection equipment must be documented. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 28 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard 7 Opportunities and Risks 7.1 This standard provides a consistent approach to addressing fall hazards at all Cleveland-Cliffs Steel facilities. 7.2 This standard provides opportunities for employees and contractors to be protected from falls to below and falling into hazardous equipment. 7.3 Risks addressed in this standard: • Working at elevated heights. • Proper design and use of fall protection equipment. • Handrail and guardrail design. • Protection of workers from falling objects. • Appropriate training for workers at risk. • Proper inspection, cleaning, and storage of fall protection equipment. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 29 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard 8 Revision History Rev. Date Summary of change Authorized by 1 9-1-2022 Initial issue K. D. Berard 2 11-3-2023 Changes are identified with a delta. • Added Reference to ANSI Z359.14 – 2014 and ANSI Z359.14 – 2021 (Self Retracting Devices). • Updated the definition of Total Fall Distance to be consistent with Class 1 and Class 2 SRL deceleration distance. • Personal fall arrest systems with connection directly to the D-ring in the middle of the back, unless the manufacturer provides an approved connector (e.g., Dual Leg Personal SRL). • Allowance for materials other than cadmium plated steel for connecting means if meeting ANSI approved, tested materials. • Added option for Travel Restraint System for Crane Runway Fall Protection. Nathan Berry ∆
