documents.extractedText: Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 1 of 29 Overhead Crane Safety Standard CLEVELAND-CLIFFS STEEL Overhead Crane Safety Standard Effective Date: 9-22-2023 Supersedes: All Previous Versions Standard No.: CCS_HSS_STD_002.2 Follow-Up Review Date: 9-22-2024 1 Purpose/Scope .......................................................................................................2 2 Responsibilities and Authorities ........................................................................... 3 3 References and Definitions ...................................................................................4 4 Resources...............................................................................................................8 5 Requirements .........................................................................................................9 6 Forms and Documented Information .................................................................. 29 7 Opportunities and Risks ...................................................................................... 29 8 Revision History ................................................................................................... 29 Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 2 of 29 Overhead Crane Safety Standard 1 Purpose/Scope This policy establishes minimum standards for activities that support the inspection, operation, maintenance, boarding/de- boarding, and other safe work practices related to crane operations. This policy applies to employees of Cleveland-Cliffs Steel business units, contractors, subcontractors and hired labor employees performing work for or on behalf of Cleveland-Cliffs Steel on premises owned, rented, or otherwise occupied by Cleveland-Cliffs Steel. The policy applies to Electric Overhead Traveling (EOT) gantry, and semi-gantry cranes including cab, pendent and radio control operated cranes. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 3 of 29 Overhead Crane Safety Standard 2 Responsibilities and Authorities This standard was jointly developed with participation from the represented workforce and management. Qualified Crane Operators Are Responsible For: • Attending crane operator training and following the requirements specified in this standard. • Performing pre-use inspections to ensure cranes are operating properly and to verify that cranes can be operated safely. • Immediately reporting any critical defects or other operational conditions that may affect the safe operation of the crane. • Obeying verbal instructions or hand signals provided by designated shop floor personnel to ensure lifts and crane movements are conducted in a safe manner that avoids potential impact to equipment, personnel, or other objects. • Safely operating cranes and avoiding movements or unsafe practices that can jeopardize the safety of personnel or risk equipment or property damage. • Keeping crane cabs free of clutter and performing necessary housekeeping. • Avoiding distractions or performing other tasks that may take the operators attention away from critical actions required to safely operate the crane. • Using horns or other audible devices to alert ground personnel of the movement of the crane. • Immediately reporting any crane related incidents including personal injuries, near misses or equipment damage events. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 4 of 29 Overhead Crane Safety Standard Qualified Ground Personnel Are Responsible For: • Maintaining awareness of crane operations in their work area and verify safe approach when entering buildings, crossing medians, exiting pulpits or working around crane lifts or other areas where crane operations are conducted. • Receiving approval from the Qualified Crane Operator and verifying conditions to ensure the safe boarding of an occupied crane. • Ensuring appropriate and recognized hand signals or approved radio communications are used to ensure coordination with Qualified Crane Operators. • Suspending crane operations when an unsafe or at-risk condition is observed. • Using sound rigging practices and when necessary, performing low/limited lifts to ensure load stability or to verify the center of gravity of a load. • Using no-touch tools when engaging/disengaging safety latches or when manipulated rigging hardware or lifting cables that are under tension. • Using tag lines or other approved no-touch tools to provide a safe distance when stabilizing, moving, or adjusting suspended loads. • Clearing non-essential personnel from an area where a lift is to be performed and keeping hands and other body parts away from potential pinch points or other hazards associated with crane movements and lifts. 3 References and Definitions References • MIOSHA General Industry R 408.12004 • OSHA 29 CFR 1910.179, Overhead and Gantry Cranes • 29 CFR 1910.181, Derricks • American Society of Mechanical Engineers. (2005). ASME B30.10: Hooks • American Society of Mechanical Engineers. (2006). ASME B30.20: Below- the-Hook Lifting Devices • American Society of Mechanical Engineers. (2016). ASME B30.2: Overhead and Gantry Cranes • MIOSHA-STD-1116 Part 18: Overhead and Gantry Cranes. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 5 of 29 Overhead Crane Safety Standard Definitions Amber flashing lights: Rotating or blinking warning lights visible to the crane operators shall be used to draw attention to temporary work platforms, ladders or mobile equipment erected or staged that do not impinge on the crane envelope. This does not apply to normal storage of ladders in the upright position or wooden access platforms that provide access to equipment such as stairs or decking. A crane shall proceed with caution past a flashing amber light maintaining maximum distance as possible with lifting devices and suspended loads. Authorized employee: An employee that has been trained on the applicable procedure and has been classified as "authorized" by management. Blue flashing lights: Rotating or blinking warning lights visible to the crane operators shall be used to draw attention to a planned work zone. A crane shall never go past a flashing blue light. Bridge: The part of a crane consisting of girders, trucks, end ties, foot walks and the driving mechanism which carries the trolley or trolleys. Competent Person, Trained and Competent. (Crane Interference Form trained and Cleveland-Cliffs steel management or designees): A person who has the necessary experience of the crane and equipment used in the lifting operation to carry out the function satisfactorily, who is capable of identifying an existing or potential hazard in surroundings, or under working conditions, that are hazardous or dangerous to an employee, and who has the authority and knowledge to initiate prompt corrective measures to eliminate the hazards and implement the Crane Interference Form (CCS_HHS_FRM_14.1). Crane – Cab-Operated Crane: A crane controlled by an operator in a cab located on the bridge or trolley. Crane – EOT Cranes (Electric Overhead Traveling): A crane with a movable bridge carrying a movable or fixed hoisting mechanism and traveling on an overhead fixed runway structure. Crane – Gantry Crane: A crane like an overhead crane except that the bridge for carrying the trolley or trolleys is rigidly supported on two or more legs running on fixed rails or another runway. Crane – Jib Cranes (Wall Crane): A crane having a jib with or without trolley and supported from a side wall or line of columns of a building. It is a traveling type and operates on a runway attached to the side wall or columns. Crane (cab operated, remote operated, pendant operated and automatic cranes, EOT Crane): Includes bridge, trolley, end trucks, cab and if applicable, permanently attached (wire rope reeved) lifting devices (block, Heppenstall, j-hooks, etc.). Crane – Automatic Crane: A crane which when activated operates through a preset cycle or cycles. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 6 of 29 Overhead Crane Safety Standard ∆ Crane Envelope: The following are the conditions defining the crane envelope: • Ten (10) feet above the trolley. • Ten (10) feet directly below and adjacent to a fixed cab. • Ten (10) feet below the bridge, unless one of the following conditions exists: a. Crane cab is mounted on the trolley, then it is ten (10) feet below the cab and across the length of the bridge. b. Ten (10) feet below the lowest part of the nested lifting device and across the length of the bridge. For example: if a set of j-hooks when nested extend 15 feet below the bridge, the envelope is 25 feet below the entire length of the bridge. Crane Lift Plan or Lifting Plan: Provides a systematic approach towards planning a lift and ensures that the lifting operation is properly managed. For example, a lifting plan would ensure that the crane is safely deployed and operated, and the lifting crew are clear about their roles and responsibilities. Critical Lift: A lift that (1) exceeds 75 percent of the rated capacity of the crane or derrick, or (2) requires the use of more than one crane or derrick. Critical Lifts, Abnormal Lifts, and High-Risk Lifts need a Crane Lift Plan. Refer to section 5.19. Designated Safe Location (applies only to planned work zones): Workers must be protected from being struck by other cranes when permission is given by safety lookouts to move through a planned work zone. The group must be positioned so that they may not be injured by movement of other cranes into or through the planned work zone when permission is given for such movement. The designated safe location may be within the crane envelope, but the crane, crane cab or the permanently attached lifting device in the nested position shall not be able strike the workers. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 7 of 29 Overhead Crane Safety Standard Extended Point: For the extent of this document, it would be the reaching point of a fully extended boom of a mobile crane or the fully extended reach of a man lift. Hot Rail: Electrical conductors (runway conductors) located along a crane runway to provide power to the crane. Impinge: To encroach, infringe on the crane envelope, to influence the crane. Impinging – Capable of Impinging: To be capable of entering into the crane envelope. Example: a 90-foot man-lift working in a building that is 100 ft. tall is capable of impinging into the crane envelope, even if it is only being used at a height of 40 feet. Limit Switch: A switch which is operated by some part or motion of a power-driven machine or equipment to alter the electric circuit associated with the machine or equipment. Load: Refers to the object(s) being hoisted and/or the weight of the object(s); both uses refer to the object(s) and the load-attaching equipment, such as, the load block, ropes, slings, shackles, and any other ancillary attachment. Load Block (Crane Block): The load block is the assembly of hook or shackle, swivel, bearing, sheaves, pins, and frame suspended by the hoisting rope. Monorail System (hoist, crane): An overhead track from which hoisting equipment travels to transport loads and includes curves, switches, transfer devices, drop sections, hangers, and related equipment. Multiple Crane Lifts: Those which involve two or more cranes to support a load either with hooks attached directly to the load by slings, through shackles attached to pad eyes or directly to an equalizer beam. Programmed Work Zone: Programmed work zone - computer program restrictions by the department and/or automation engineers that sets crane(s) operational boundaries for automatic cranes. Qualified Crane Operator: A person who has been trained in the operation, function and testing of the crane that has successfully demonstrated the ability to operate the crane and has been deemed qualified and assigned by management as the principal operator of the crane. Qualified Floor Person: A person who, by possession of a recognized degree, certificate, or professional standing, or who by extensive knowledge or training and experience, successfully demonstrated the ability to solve/resolve problems related to the subject matter, the work, or the project. Rail Stop (rail dog): A device attached to a crane bridge rail or fixed structure to limit the travel of the crane bridge. Safety Latch: A hook with a latch to prevent slings or load from accidentally slipping off the hook. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 8 of 29 Overhead Crane Safety Standard Safety Lookout: A person whose sole responsibility is to look out for the crew or crews being protected and to prohibit the crane operator (one Lookout per crane) from operating the crane too close to the personnel being protected. The safety lookout is assigned to the group doing the repair or maintenance activity. This person reports to and is relieved with the work group. The safety lookout may be positioned in the crane cab or on the ground with the work crew based on the circumstances of the work to be done. One safety look out will be assigned to each crane on either side of the work area. Side Pull, Side Swing: The portion of the hoist pull acting horizontally when the hoist lines are not operated vertically. Suspended Load: Anything that is lifted above ground level. Trolley: The unit which travels on the bridge rails and carries the hoisting mechanism. Work Group Supervisor or Leader: The individual in charge of the work that is to be performed. In most cases this is not the operations supervisor but the repair group supervisor doing the work activity. 4 Resources None Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 9 of 29 Overhead Crane Safety Standard ∆ 5 Requirements Medical Qualifications 5.1.1 Only trained and authorized personnel are allowed to operate a crane. Qualification as a crane operator shall be based on medical certification, training and demonstrated ability to operate any crane to which the employee may be assigned. Cranes shall be operated in a competent manner in strict compliance with government regulations and all applicable crane safety rules. 5.1.2 All crane operators must be deemed medically qualified to operate any crane. General Crane Awareness Training 5.2.1 All employees shall be trained at least to an awareness level on crane safety and the requirements within this standard. 5.2.2 Cleveland-Cliffs Steel managers and designees, affected employees shall be trained initially prior to assignment and whenever there is a significant change in this standard and shall be trained in the following: 5.2.2.1 Crane Interference Form requirements: • How to properly complete and implement Crane Interference Form (CCS_HHS_FRM_14.1). 5.2.3 Safety lookouts shall be trained in the following: • The location and boundaries of the work area. • Specific responsibilities, duties, and obligations to the work crew. • The signs and signals of the job. • Responsibility of not leaving the job until relieved by the work crew supervisor or leader. Initial Training 5.3.1 All newly assigned crane operators must attend formal basic skills training including classroom and hands-on training. Each crane operator must successfully complete a defined period of on-the-job training and a performance evaluation under the direction of designated approved trainers prior to being qualified as a crane operator. 5.3.2 The successful completion of training shall include documentation (e.g., quiz or post-training test) that the crane operator has acquired the understanding, knowledge, and skills necessary to safely perform their duties. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 10 of 29 Overhead Crane Safety Standard ∆ 5.3.3 Training shall include: • The operator's responsibility is to perform and document a pre-use inspection of the crane. • Basic design and operating functions of cranes. • Limit switch testing. • Proper execution of each specific lifting procedure, including: a. Environmental hazards – weather b. Pre-use inspections/tests c. Load weight estimation d. Emergency procedures e. Traveling with load control f. Rigging g. Hand signals h. Load dynamics i. Limit switches j. Warning signals k. How to properly complete and implement the Crane Interference Form (CCS_HHS_FRM_14.1). l. Responsibilities of the safety lookout 5.3.4 Refresher training must be provided under the following circumstances: • Observation of unsafe operation of the crane. • Operator was involved in an accident or a near-miss incident. • Conditions in the workplace or equipment change in a manner that could affect the safe operation of the crane. • An extended period in which the operator has not operated a crane and feels they need refresher training. Note: the exact content and duration of refresher training will be specific to and consistent with the circumstances above. What is necessary to close any training and operating skills gaps is the question that must be satisfied. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 11 of 29 Overhead Crane Safety Standard 5.3.5 The successful completion of training shall include documentation (e.g., quiz or post-training test) that the crane operator has acquired the understanding, knowledge, and skills necessary to safely perform their duties. 5.3.6 A documented crane evaluation form shall also be used to document completion of a crane operator’s on-the-job training and their ability to safely perform the required crane operations associated with their crane assignment. 5.3.7 Rigging training must include the following: a. Select tackle and hardware suitable to the load. b. Environmental hazards – weather. c. Inspection/tests. d. Load weight estimation. e. Rigging equipment selection. f. Hand signals. g. Maintenance/storage of slings and rigging components. h. Rigging/operating safe practices. i. Load-indicating devices. j. Personal protective equipment. Training Documentation 5.4.1 All training must be documented as either initial or refresher and maintained for the period that all other training records are maintained (both immediately accessible or via archives) per each business unit’s practice. Crane Boarding/De-Boarding 5.5.1 Crane boarding that involves a host department and a service department employee or crew must be coordinated so that the host department is aware of the activity and can provide further guidance on any issues/scheduling of the crane in question. Full and on-going communications is required. 5.5.2 Fall protection requirements both fixed and personal must be discussed and implemented. 5.5.3 No one shall ever board or de-board a moving crane. 5.5.4 Personnel, other than qualified crane operators, shall not be permitted on cranes, crane runways or in crane cabs without the authorization of management. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 12 of 29 Overhead Crane Safety Standard ∆ ∆ 5.5.5 Verify status lights before boarding any crane. Status lights shall be visible from the boarding platform. 5.5.6 Sites can establish and train personnel on the site’s standard for crane status light colors. 5.5.7 The site’s standard configuration for crane power and magnet power is arranged to include a fail-safe so that the status can be determined if a light is not functioning. (e.g., magnet indicator light is off to indicate power is on.) 5.5.8 A documented procedure for boarding and de-boarding occupied and unoccupied overhead cranes shall be developed and implemented. The procedure shall have, at minimum, the following instruction: Boarding a Crane That is Occupied 5.6.1 The authorized employee shall notify the crane operator of their intention to board the crane and shall receive acknowledgement from the crane operator. 5.6.2 The crane operator shall de-energize the crane. 5.6.3 The crane operator shall assure the crane power OFF indicator status light is lit and then place the OK to board indicator light to ON if the crane is so equipped. 5.6.4 The crane operator shall then exit the cab and go to a position where they can be seen by the employee(s) wishing to board the crane. 5.6.5 The crane operator may put the crane into operation only after ensuring all employees are clear, the Crane Power ON light is turned on and sounds the crane warning for at least five seconds. General Crane Rules 5.14.1 Crane operators shall not make or complete a lift where: a. Line of sight to the load or lifting device can-not be maintained, unless directed by authorized personnel. b. Instruct the work crew to position all equipment out of the incoming crane's envelope. 2. Move to a designated safe location which ensures the work crew will not be struck by the overhead crane as the crane travels into or through the planned work zone. 3. Receive confirmation that the work crew has moved to the designated safe location and all pieces of equipment are outside of the incoming crane’s envelope. 4. Turn off the flashing blue light and communicate with the crane to pass or travel into the protected work zone. 5. After the crane has exited out of the planned work zone, the blue flashing lights shall be reactivated. 6. Contact the crane operators that the planned work zone is active again. 5.26.14 Riding outside the cab or landing platform is prohibited except for inspection and adjustment of parts, or where necessary in the performance of maintenance work. Riding on the trolley while the crane is in motion is never permitted. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 28 of 29 Overhead Crane Safety Standard 5.26.15 Persons checking the performance of the crane while it is in operation shall have: a. Department clearance accompanied with a written procedure signed by the maintenance shift supervisor. b. A clear understanding and communication with the crane operator of the position(s) of the service people. c. All other motions, other than the one being checked, shall be locked out, or the crane operator in the cab, in communication with the repair person, and instructed by the repair person. 5.26.16 A person must guide all travel of any Cleveland-Cliffs Steel owned or contractor owned mobile crane entering or operating, in any building, in which overhead cranes are operating. Working on Cranes 5.27.1 Prior to commencing any preventative, break down or shutdown maintenance on an overhead crane, a Red Pennant Flag (highly visible) must be lowered from the crane 10 to 15 feet above the floor. 5.27.2 The pennant shall have "WARNING" displayed on both sides and shall easily be seen from the floor. 5.27.3 Warning signs shall also be placed on the floor (i.e., "Caution Overhead Work") to alert others in the area of the work being performed on the crane overhead. 5.27.4 The warning signs will be the maximum protection required if there is no potential for tools, parts, or materials to fall to the area below. 5.27.5 A Red Danger Tape Zone (with identification, i.e., department name, Contractor name) shall be erected to completely encompass and block access to work areas on the ground when there is a potential for tools, parts, or materials to fall from the crane during the maintenance activity. 5.27.6 Entry into the Red Zone shall be prohibited during the maintenance activity. 5.27.7 Entry into the Red Zone shall be prohibited until all conditions are controlled. Prior to Entry permission must be granted by work group. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 29 of 29 Overhead Crane Safety Standard ∆ 6 Forms and Documented Information Crane Interference Form - CCS_HHS_FRM_14.1 Crane Pre-use Inspection Checklist - CCS_HHS_FRM_13.2 7 Opportunities and Risks This document provides the framework to reduce the likelihood of an overhead crane related injury. The risks addressed in this standard are: • Working at heights • Control of hazardous energy • Dropped objects • Caught by/caught between hazards 8 Revision History Rev. Date Summary of change Authorized by 1 9-1-2022 Initial issue K. D. Berard 2 9-22-2023 Changes are identified with a delta. • Clarification of when a lift plan is needed. • Clarification that a crane trainee will need to pass a test. • Added Crane Interference Form to crane training. • Changed the crane status light color requirement to have sites establish a plant standard light system. Require training on the site’s standard colors. • Added the requirement to remove a below the hook device prior to an upper limit test (pre-shift). • Added basic elements of periodic, annual, and cranes not in regular use inspection elements. • Comment regarding people with pacemakers not working in close proximity to strong magnetic fields. • Other minor editorial modifications. Dirk Berard Senior Director Health Safety Security 11/14/2022 APPROVER DATE 1 Purpose/Scope ........................................................................................................ 2 2 Responsibilities and Authorities ............................................................................... 3 3 References .............................................................................................................. 3 4 Resources ................................................................................................................ 4 5 Requirements .......................................................................................................... 5 6 Index ...................................................................................................................... 38 7 Revision History ..................................................................................................... 39 Safety Handbook For reference only. Page 2 of 39 1 Purpose/Scope This Handbook establishes minimum standards for Personal protective equipment, Ariel lifts and Scissor lifts, Entering Buildings / Departments, Excavations, Floors and Pit Openings Fire Prevention and Firefighting, General Requirements, Housekeeping, Incident Investigation Industrial Vehicles: Operation and Care, Ladders, Scaffolding and Staging, Personal Protective Equipment, Personal Vehicles, Powered Hand Tools and Fixed Equipment, Safe Storing, Loading and Manual Handing of Material, Three-Part Communication, Use and Care of Hand Tools, Use of Tape for Hazard Demarcation, Walkways, Work Areas, Roadways, Stairs and Doors Welding Burning and Cutting, Working at Overhead Locations. This policy applies to employees of Cleveland-Cliffs Steel business units, contractors, subcontractors and hired labor employees performing work for or on behalf of Cleveland-Cliffs Steel on premises owned, rented or otherwise occupied by Cleveland-Cliffs Steel. Safety Handbook For reference only. Invalid if printed. Page 3 of 39 2 Responsibilities and Authorities This standard was jointly developed with participation from the represented workforce and management. Each facilities management is responsible for the implementation of this standard. The Senior Director of Health, Safety and Security is responsible for authorizing this standard. 3 References References  CCS_HSS_STD_001.1 Energy Isolation Safety Standard  CCS_HSS_STD_002.1 Overhead Crane Safety Standard  CCS_HSS_STD_003.1 Rail Safety Standard  CCS_HSS_STD_004.1 Confined Space Safety Standard  CCS_HSS_STD_005.1 Fall Protection Safety Standard  CCS_HSS_STD_006.1 Aerial Lifts Safety Standard  CCS_HSS_STD_007.1 Mobile Equipment Safety Standard  CCS_HSS_STD_008.1 Tool Safety Standard  CCS_HSS_STD_009.1 Cutting, Burning, and Welding Safety Standard  1910.67 Aerial Lifts and Mobile Work Platforms  1910.252 Welding Burning and Brazing  1910.176 Material Handling Safety Handbook For reference only. Invalid if printed. Page 4 of 39  1910.141 General Environmental Controls  1910.132 Personal Protective Equipment  ANSI Z-89.1  ASTM-F2413  ANSI Z.87  ANSI 105  NIOSH 42 CFR 84 4 Resources None Safety Handbook For reference only. Invalid if printed. Page 5 of 39 5 Requirements General Requirements 5.1.1 Employees must report to work “Fit for Duty”  A state which enables the employee to perform assigned tasks competently and in a manner which does not compromise or threatens the safety of health of yourselves or others. 5.1.2 Keep yourself or others outside the “Line of Fire”  Pinch points, release of hazardous energy, beneath the path of dropped objects, path of mobile equipment etc. 5.1.3 Horseplay, startling, teasing, throwing of objects, scuffling or distracting another employee is strictly prohibited. 5.1.4 Never lean against, sit, or stand, on temporary hand railings or guard railings of any kind. 5.1.5 Before sitting in a chair assure that it is in good repair (including all of the legs) and that is placed on a flat level surface, with all of the legs making contact with the floor surface.  While sitting in a chair, never tip the chair to cause one or more of the chair legs to lose contact with the floor surface.  While sitting in a chair, never prop your feet on a surface above the level of the seat or in any other way that will cause the chair to become unstable.  Chairs with a single post and a base shall have a minimum of 5 legs, with or without casters, originating from the center post 5.1.6 Never dispose of empty aerosol cans or gas cylinders in dumpsters or containers in which they could end up in molten metal, scrap, or be exposed to heat. 5.1.7 Intercoms, PA Systems and Two-way radios are to be used for business purposes only. Non-essential communication and inappropriate language are prohibited. 5.1.8 Cell phones and laptop computers provided by the company and used to conduct business may be carried on the plant property and into operating areas.  Cell phones with photographic or video capabilities shall not be used for taking photographs or videos on company property unless authorized by Cleveland-Cliffs Steel management.  Cell phones or electronic devices shall not be used in operating areas. Employees must move to a safe location before using these devices. Safety Handbook For reference only. Invalid if printed. Page 6 of 39 5.1.9 When operating a company-owned vehicle, rental vehicle, leased vehicle or personal vehicle, while performing company business, drivers shall not operate a cell phone, electronic communication device or any other electronic equipment, that is NOT "Hands-Free" equipped.  The term “Hands-free" equipped is defined as an attachment, add-on, built-in feature or addition to a mobile cellular telephone that, when used, allows the driver to maintain both hands on the steering wheel when receiving, talking and terminating a cellular call. The hands-free accessory can be either permanently installed in the vehicle or may be portable.  This rule shall apply to company-owned/issued devices or ones owned by the employee.  If an employee must utilize a cell phone or tablet that are not “Hands-free” they shall drive to a safe location and stop the vehicle prior to activating the device, remaining there until the communication is completed. Personal Vehicles 5.2.1 Anyone on a motorcycle shall be wearing an approved motorcycle helmet according to local and state laws and/or plant specific policy.  Motorcycles are only permitted to be ridden and parked in Cleveland-Cliffs Steel approved locations. 5.2.2 Obey posted signs (speed limit, parking areas, directional signs, etc.) 5.2.3 No personal trailers, boats, campers, etc. allowed on property without written approval by plant general manager or designee. 5.2.4 If a personal vehicle becomes disabled on Cleveland-Cliffs Steel property, employees are not permitted to work on the vehicle, but must call an (outside) Road Service to respond.  Note: This restriction does not apply to simple repairs, such as changing a flat tire, jump starting a dead battery, and third-party windshield repair. Entering Buildings / Departments 5.3.1 Do not go into any department, other than your own, unless your work requires you to do so. 5.3.2 Sign in and out as required by the department prior to entering and after exiting the operations area. 5.3.3 When going into other departments contact the appropriate department person at the sign in location and comply with that department's safety rules, including the wearing of all appropriate personal protective equipment. Safety Handbook For reference only. Invalid if printed. Page 7 of 39 5.3.4 Always enter through designated man doors.  It is only permitted to enter through a roll-up door, if a man door is not present and the door has been pinned, posted and operational control is locked out. 5.3.5 When entering a building, stop and assess operational conditions and possible movement of overhead cranes or other mobile equipment before proceeding. Do not assume that crane or mobile equipment operators can see you. 5.3.6 Warning signs and warning signal systems have been established in each department. Know and obey the signs and signals of the department where you work and those of any department that your work requires you to enter. 5.3.7 Signals - Make sure you know the Emergency Signals and Evacuation Plans in each department where you work. Incident Investigation 5.4.1 Report all work-related injuries, occupational illnesses, near misses and equipment, product and property damage incidents to Cleveland-Cliffs Steel Management immediately.  If a work-related injury or illness is not immediately apparent, it shall be reported as soon as the injury or illness is discovered. 5.4.2 Employees have the right to report work-related injuries and illnesses; and employers are prohibited from discharging or in any manner discriminating against employees for reporting work-related injuries or illnesses. 5.4.3 All involved employees are required to cooperate with management, union safety advocates /coordinators, and other people investigating any incidents or exposures. When asked about an incident with injury/incident/exposure, provide detailed factual information of what was witnessed. This will include:  All perishable evidence must be preserved  Interviews  Statements  Photos/videos 5.4.4 Emergency Reporting Procedures and Emergency Action Plan must be followed. Safety Handbook For reference only. Invalid if printed. Page 8 of 39 Three-Part Communication 5.5.1 Three-part communication shall be included in all applicable Job Safety Procedures and when the actions of another person is affected. Applicable Job Safety Procedures shall include, LOTOs, temporary work instruction, crane boarding/ de- boarding requirements etc. or where more than one person or crew is working together on a task. 5.5.2 Anytime more than one person or crew is involved in a task that requires understanding and coordination between the two, clear and concise “Initiate- Acknowledge-Confirm (IAC)” communication shall be utilized in the following manner:  Employee 1 – Initiates communication.  Employee 2 – Acknowledges by repeating the message.  Employee 1 – Confirms that Employee 2 received the correct message. 5.5.3 All work shall PAUSE if any of the three parts of IAC are not clearly understood (i.e., employee 1 does not initiate the communication, employee 2 does not acknowledge the initial communication, or employee 1 does not confirm correct understanding from employee 2). 5.5.4 Avoid using single word responses that could be easily confused such as “Go” and “No” or using phrases that end in an action that rely a single word such as “Clear” or “Not clear”. Use words like negative, positive, or phrases that repeat the emphasis sentence such as “We are not, I repeat, not clear.” 5.5.5 Any confusion in communications should result in a pause of work to clarify what is being said and what actions need to occur. Housekeeping 5.6.1 Keep your work area clean and clear. Pick up and dispose of debris as it accumulates. Return hand tools and equipment to their proper storage places when finished with them.  Keep all walkways, aisles, stairs, and platforms clear of obstructions. Do not pile materials in any area where people must walk. Be sure that materials which are stacked or piled near walkways do not project into aisles, stairs or platforms and that they are properly stacked so they will not topple or fall.  Do not obstruct access to emergency exits, fixed ladders, stairways, electrical switches, shutoff valves, firefighting or rescue equipment and safety eyewash fountains or safety showers. Do not store any material in, on, or in front of switch boxes or other electrical equipment. Safety Handbook For reference only. Invalid if printed. Page 9 of 39 5.6.2 When you have completed repair, construction, or maintenance work of any kind, take time to clean the area. Pick up and remove all waste and salvaged materials. Return all hand tools and equipment to proper storage. Remove all loose objects after completing overhead work. Replace all covers, guards and/or access panels. 5.6.3 Containers shall be provided for the collection and separation of waste, trash, and other refuse. Containers used for oily, flammable, or hazardous wastes (such as caustics, acids, harmful dust, etc.) shall be equipped with covers and labeled. Garbage and other waste shall be disposed of at frequent and regular intervals. Never dispose of trash or non-metallic waste in scrap metal containers.  When working with, moving or cleaning materials such as metal, wood, glass, etc., do not use your hands, forearms, or other parts of your body to remove slag, slivers, chips, dust, etc. from materials or surrounding areas. 5.6.4 Each plant shall develop a housekeeping program, which at a minimum must include a monthly area housekeeping inspection. Personal Clothing / Jewelry 5.7.1 Employee’s bodies shall be covered during work hours to comply with department and plant regulations. Only approved apparel, worn in the proper manner shall be permitted in the plant. 5.7.2 Pants must extend at least to the ankles. 5.7.3 Long sleeved shirts are required in all operating areas with the sleeves down and buttoned at the wrist. The shirt shall be tucked into the trousers and fully buttoned up the front to the first button below the collar button. The collar button shall be buttoned when directed by specific Department Procedures. Exceptions to this rule:  This rule does not apply to non-operating areas such as office areas, break rooms, general office buildings, etc.  Permitting rolled up long sleeves in operating areas (Machine Shops. Etc.), shall be documented in writing and approved by the Plant Manager and Safety Department. 5.7.4 Work clothes shall not be cleaned in flammable liquids, such as gasoline, kerosene, or similar fluids. 5.7.5 Synthetic clothing including under clothing, that is not made of approved fire retardant or fire-resistant materials, shall not be worn in hot metal areas or when exposed to burning, welding, flame, high radiant heat areas or potential arc flash. 5.7.6 Do not wear clothing that is loose fitting, torn, or ragged, too long (pant legs/shirt sleeves) or with attached hoods (i.e., hooded sweatshirts) to avoid being caught on projections or in moving machinery. Safety Handbook For reference only. Invalid if printed. Page 10 of 39 5.7.7 Permanently affixed hooded garments are not permitted unless a documented hazard assessment has been conducted and requirement is specified in a Job Safety Procedure. (I.e., hooded tap coats, disposable coveralls, etc.) 5.7.8 Wearing of finger rings (including silicone or rubber rings), loose-fitting wrist bracelets, exposed dangling necklaces, and dangling earrings or nose rings, other than stud type earrings, or having gauged ear lobes that are open, are prohibited in all operating areas.  Stud type earrings are permitted in the operating areas as long as they are single studs and fit directly over the opening in the ear lobe and do not project up or down in any manner.  Gauged ear lobes that have the hole plugged with a solid blank or covered with tape or a Band-Aid are permitted.  All earrings and gauged lobes must be covered with tape or a Band-Aid while performing any type of electrical work. 5.7.9 Employees with shoulder length or longer hair, or long facial hair (beards) shall be maintained / secured so that it does not create a hazard. Personal Protective Equipment 5.8.1 Cleveland-Cliffs Steel employees shall be trained on the proper inspection and use of all Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) issued to them.  Unauthorized alterations of personal protective equipment in any way are strictly prohibited. 5.8.2 All Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) must follow manufacturer’s recommendations and requirements. 5.8.3 Always inspect the PPE before use and replace if needed. Report defects to Cleveland-Cliffs Steel Management immediately. 5.8.4 Cleveland-Cliffs Steel employees are not permitted to use PPE on Cleveland-Cliffs Steel property that were not approved and provided by Cleveland-Cliffs. 5.8.5 Job Safety Procedures or Department Rules shall specify the PPE required for each job. If the PPE is not identified, contact Cleveland-Cliffs Steel Management to confirm PPE requirements before starting the task or if the task’s conditions have changed and may require additional PPE. 5.8.6 Persons working within 10 feet of a body of water, 4 feet or greater in depth, shall wear an approved PFD (personal floatation device), if not protected by handrail or other fall protection. Safety Handbook For reference only. Invalid if printed. Page 11 of 39 5.8.7 Protective Helmets 5.8.8 Only Cleveland-Cliffs Steel approved Protective helmets conforming to ANSI Z-89.1 Industrial Standard shall be worn. Your protective helmet shall:  Be worn with bill to the front. Unless an approved exception is documented in a hazard assessment and Job Safety Procedure.  Without altering or wearing anything that would affect the suspension system.  Hats (baseball type hats, tassel caps, toboggans, etc.) that may affect the fit of the helmet shall not be worn under the protective helmet. Welders’ caps, liners or other tight fitting garment that do not affect the hat hard suspension are permitted to be worn under the helmets.  Without painting, drilling, or otherwise altering the helmet shell.  With your first and last name printed or labeled onto the front of the helmet.  With reflective safety tape as follows: · At least a three (3) inch long strip on each side and back of the helmet placed approximately one (1) inch up from the brim of the hat.  Hardhat or suspension cracked, chipped, burnt, or otherwise suspected to be damaged shall be taken out of service immediately.  Employees operating or riding in enclosed crane cabs or mobile equipment are not required to wear hard hats unless directed to do so by a specific Job Safety Procedure.  A red flashing light placed where visible is required to enter designated coil fields, low visibility situations and/or as specified in a Job Safety Procedure. (I.e. roll storage racks, slab yards, batch annealing operations, etc.) 5.8.9 Metatarsal Boots  Only Cleveland-Cliffs Steel approved six inch or higher, safety toe, safety boots with permanently attached or internal metatarsal guards conforming to ANSI Z-41 Industrial Standard in good repair, properly laced and tied shall be worn by Cleveland-Cliffs Steel employees.  Cleveland-Cliffs Steel employees are only permitted to obtain metatarsal boots through Cleveland-Cliffs Steel approved metatarsal boot vendors.  Rubber type metatarsal boots are not permitted unless required by the Job Safety Procedure.  Temporary metatarsal guards are not permitted. Safety Handbook For reference only. Invalid if printed. Page 12 of 39 5.8.10 Safety Glasses 5.8.11 Only Cleveland-Cliffs Steel approved safety plastic framed glasses with permanently attached side shields or wrap around design which meet the ANSI Z.87 Industrial Standard shall be worn by Cleveland-Cliffs Steel employees.  Employees are only permitted to obtain prescription safety glasses through Cleveland-Cliffs Steel approved eye glass vendors.  Additional eye protection, such as face shields, welding helmets, goggles, etc., may be required for specific jobs. Always wear the type of eye protection prescribed for the job as specified by the Job Safety Procedure.  Employees operating or riding in fully enclosed crane cabs or mobile equipment with all windows closed are not required to wear approved safety glasses unless directed to do so by a specific Job Safety Procedure.  Sunglasses, mirrored sunglasses, transition glasses, etc. are not permitted to be worn inside the plant. Prescription exemptions and or medical conditions must be documented in writing and be approved by the employee's doctor / plant medical and the Safety Department Employees performing tasks identified in the Job Safety Procedure requiring dark lenses shall be provided the appropriate glasses, clip-ons, flip downs, goggles, face shields, or hoods. 5.8.12 Face Protection 5.8.13 Only Cleveland-Cliffs Steel approved face shields which meet the ANSI Z.87 Industrial Standard shall be worn. 5.8.14 The material constructing the face shield shall be selected based on the potential hazard. Solid material (polycarbonate, acetate, etc.) face shields shall be worn when the hazards is either liquid, molten, arc flash, impact or steam. 5.8.15 Face shields shall be worn in addition to approved safety glasses or goggles. 5.8.16 A face shield shall be worn in the down position if the work activity includes one or more of the following hazards:  Handling metal or plastic banding while banding coils or other materials, picking up and carrying loose bands or when cutting bands from coils, bundles, pallets, etc. (> 6 inches in length).  Employees within an arms' length of metal ends, samples, scrap or other materials that can whip or spring, striking the face (I.e. edge trim, weld scarf, scrap bales, flashing).  Handling full width samples or scrap. Safety Handbook For reference only. Invalid if printed. Page 13 of 39  Exposure to flame, sparks, ultraviolet radiation (welding) arc flash or radiant heat as defined in a hazard assessment.  Exposure to molten metal (zinc, aluminum, steel, iron, etc.).  Exposure to acidic, caustic, hot and/or cryogenic fluids  Spraying with pressurized (>25 psi) liquids, air and mixtures. (I.e. refractory gunning, pressure washing, cleaning via water hose, abrasive blasting, etc.).  Exposure to steam  When performing work that could cause deposited dust or metal fines to drop down onto the employee(s).  Grinding, chipping, striking or cutting operations that cause flying sparks, chips or particles.  While troubleshooting and/or performing maintenance on hydraulic, pneumatic, steam, or any other line that is under pressure.  As required by the Job Safety Procedure or department rules. 5.8.17 When working in chemical areas where the procedure requires a chemical barrier suit, the face shield shall be equipped with a chin cup protector to enhance protection to the face and neck. In addition, goggles shall be worn under the face shield for added protection to the eyes. 5.8.18 Respiratory Protection 5.8.19 Only Cleveland-Cliffs Steel designated NIOSH approved respiratory protection shall be worn.  If wearing a respirator is required, you must be medically evaluated, fit tested and properly trained.  Facial hair or stubble shall be trimmed or shaved to ensure an adequate seal and proper function of the respirator  Respirators must be stored per the manufacturers requirements  Employees shall inspect their respirators prior to use.  Employees shall conduct field verification (positive and negative) fit checks prior to entering the respiratory required work area. 5.8.20 Voluntary use of respiratory protection requires the employee to be provided a copy of Appendix D to Sec. 1910.134 (Mandatory) Information for Employees Using Respirators When Not Required under the Standard. 5.8.21 Hand Protection Safety Handbook For reference only. Invalid if printed. Page 14 of 39  Before handling any object, substance, or tool, approved hand protection shall be selected and worn to provide the required level of protection.  Hand protection shall be selected based on an evaluation of the performance characteristics of the equipment relative to the job tasks to be performed and the type of hazard/hazards associated with the tasks.  Approved and designated cut resistant gloves shall be properly worn when the employee is within an arm’s length of cut hazard from coils, metal strips, banding, scrap, etc. or as directed by the Job Safety Procedure or department rules.  At a minimum, approved leather palmed puncture resistant gloves shall be properly worn when handling wire rope, wire slings or other materials with a potential puncture hazard or as directed by the Job Safety Procedure or Department Rules.  Hand protection shall be designated in a Job Safety Procedure or by department rules and shall be worn as required.  Hand protection shall be worn as designed by the manufacturer and shall not be altered from the original design. 5.8.22 Arm Protection 5.8.23 All employees wear Cut resistant sleeves when within arm’s length of coils, samples, strip, scrap, or other cut hazards; or when directed by a Job Safety Procedure.  Cut resistant sleeves are not required after a PPE hazard assessment has been performed and there is no exposure to cut hazard.  Cut resistant sleeves shall be worn with the thumb through the thumbhole and finger(s) through the finger hole(s) and worn under gloves when required  The Cut resistant sleeves must be extended above the elbow, where they shall be secured with the clips or in such a manner that the Cut resistant sleeves will remain in place. 5.8.24 Torso and Leg Protection  Full length cut-resistant chaps shall be worn whenever the employee is within an arm’s length of coils, metal strip, scrap, banding, or other similar cut hazards.  Full length cut resistant chaps shall be worn when walking/working in designated coil fields or as required by a Job Safety Procedure. Safety Handbook For reference only. Invalid if printed. Page 15 of 39  Cut-resistant aprons shall be worn when there is a potential to strike the torso against protruding metal strip, scrap, banding, or other similar cut hazards or as required by a Job Safety Procedure.  Aprons shall not be worn when there is a potential of being caught in machinery. 5.8.25 High Heat Exposure Clothing  Approved aluminized coat, or equivalent material, completely secured, shall be worn to protect the base of the neck, torso, arms and upper legs from radiant heat, molten metal, and metal red zones or as required by a Job Safety Procedure and/or department rules and shall extend at least 2 inches over the spats.  Approved aluminized, or other equivalent material, spats shall be worn to protect from the top of the foot to the knee from radiant heat, molten metal and sparks or as required by a Job Safety Procedure.  The spats may be worn under the outer garment or over the outer garment in the following manner: Non-Aluminized spats worn under approved flame-retardant pants or coveralls shall be worn over approved under garments to provide additional protection from the hot work hazards and to prevent skin irritation. Aluminized spats worn over approved issued uniform shall have a minimum of one inch of the pant leg blousing out and over the top of the main body section of the leggings  Approved aluminized or equivalent material jacket with reflective tape with hood, completely secured and hood over helmet, shall be worn to protect the head, neck and torso of the railroad crew within 30 feet of torpedo cars transporting molten iron.  The aluminized jacket requirements do not apply to burning or brazing with a hand torch or hand held welding or air arcing unless specifically required by a Job Safety Procedure.  Approved aluminized neck shroud or equivalent material shall be properly worn in conjunction with an approved face shield and carbonex type hood when there is a molten metal splash hazard or as required by the Job Safety Procedure. Safety Handbook For reference only. Invalid if printed. Page 16 of 39  Approved aluminized or equivalent material beehive type hood shall be worn when the combination of a face shield, aluminized shroud and carbonex type hood does not provide adequate protection from exposures to molten metal, sparks, radiant heat, flame and/or steam or as required by the Job Safety Procedure.  Approved long cuff gloves with cinches when worn over the aluminized or equivalent material coat shall be cinched tight.  Approved or equivalent material gloves without cinches shall be worn under the aluminized or equivalent material coat sleeves and the coat sleeves with Velcro closure or snaps shall be tightened or snapped over the gloves. 5.8.26 Minimum PPE  Cleveland-Cliffs Steel issued uniform:  FR ankle length pants, FR wrist length shirt (Hot metal uniforms pant Hot metal uniforms shirts in all department’s where molten metal is present)  Hard hat  Safety eyewear  Metatarsal boots with safety toe  Appropriate gloves for the task  Hearing protection where required 5.8.27 Coil fields or working within arm length of a coil In addition to minimum PPE, when interacting with coils where there is a potential to strike against or be struck by protruding metal strip, scrap, banding, or other similar cut hazards or as required by a Job Safety Procedure.  Cut resistant chaps  Cut resistant bib/apron  Cut resistant sleeves  ANSI cut level 5 gloves  Face shield 5.8.28 Hot metal PPE In addition to minimum PPE, when interacting with molten metal or positioned in a designated molten metal red zone area, the following PPE is required:  Base layer (Carbon armor, CarbonX, DRIFIRE)* Optional Safety Handbook For reference only. Invalid if printed. Page 17 of 39  Aluminized or equivalent material Tap coat  Aluminized or equivalent material Spats  Aluminized or equivalent material Gloves  CarbonX hood  Aluminized or equivalent material neck drape  Face shield  Aluminized or equivalent material Beehive hood if job task requires based on the hazard assessment or Job Safety Procedure as required. 5.8.29 Hot Work In addition to minimum PPE, when conducting Hot Work activities the following PPE is required:  Double layer FR (FR welding jacket or leather welding jacket)  Face shield / Welding helmet (attached to hard hat or integrated into the design)  FR hood (if hot work is being performed above shoulder height)  Hot work or welding gloves  Leather or Equivalent spats 5.8.30 Any employee within 6’ shall wear the exact PPE as the employee performing the welding, burning, and cutting. Fire Prevention and Firefighting 5.9.1 Include emergency response to fires  In addition to the information below, sites are required to develop and maintain emergency action plans that include emergency response to fires. 5.9.2 Prevent Fires 5.9.3 Follow fire prevention rules for your area and be alert to potential fire hazards throughout the plant. Be aware that the danger of fires is higher in certain areas of the plant and special precautions must be taken. Know the proper way of responding to a fire and how to turn in an alarm or initiate the sites emergency notification procedure in the area where you are working. Know the emergency escape routes and the designated assembly points should evacuation become necessary. Safety Handbook For reference only. Invalid if printed. The pendant shall have "WARNING" displayed on both sides and shall easily be seen from the floor.  Warning signs shall also be placed on the floor (i.e., "Caution Overhead Work") to alert others in the area of the work being performed on the crane overhead.  The warning signs will be the maximum protection required if there is no potential for tools, parts, or materials to fall to the area below. Employees and contractors shall use caution when walking under any part of an overhead crane that has the red pendant "WARNING" flag displayed and warning signs on the floor indicating the crane is down for maintenance.  A Red Danger Tape Zone (with identification, i.e., department name, contractor name) shall be erected to completely encompass and block access to work areas on the ground when there is a potential for tools, parts or materials to fall from the crane during the maintenance activity. Entry into the Red Zone shall be prohibited during the maintenance activity. Ladders, Scaffolding and Staging 5.19.1 Extension Ladders  Always inspect ladders before use. Defective ladders shall be tagged and immediately removed from service. Notify your supervisor for a replacement.  Extension ladders are required to be inspected annually and documented.  Extension ladders must be labeled with load capacity clearly marked and visible  Portable metal ladders including aluminum shall not be approved for use.  Never paint or use painted wooden ladders. Paint will hide cracks, knots, rot, or other defects.  Straight portable ladders and extension ladders shall extend at least three feet above the top access level and be placed so the distance from the base of the ladder to the wall or other supporting structure is about one-quarter the length of the ladder from the floor to the top support point. These ladders are to be tied in place.  Both rails of the extension ladder must be tied off to a structure capable of stabilizing and supporting the ladder from falling. If the ladder cannot be tied off it must be held by a coworker whenever someone is working on the ladder. Safety Handbook For reference only. Invalid if printed. Examples are:  Both feet and 1 hand - on the ladder, belt buckle or midline of the body must be between the rails of the ladder, and the shoulders below the top rail. Any stretching for position requires repositioning of the ladder.  Both legs and body leading against the ladder. The belt buckle/midline of the body must be between rails. Any stretching for position perpendicular to the ladder requires repositioning of the ladder. Feet must be firmly on the ladder and the belt buckle/midline of the body must be resting on the ladder. The shoulders must be below the top rung. Worker may use two hands for short duration work (changing light bulbs, opening hand valves, etc.). 5.19.3 Step ladders  Step ladders are required to be inspected annually and documented.  Step ladder must be labeled with load capacity clearly marked and visible  Shall be fully opened and locked.  Never stand on top of a step ladder.  Work from a point at least two feet or two steps from the top. 5.19.4 When climbing any ladder (portable or stationary),  Hold on with both hands and always face the ladder.  Use a hand line to raise or lower tools that you will need.  Never exceed the maximum intended load of the ladder. 5.19.5 Scaffolding & Staging. 5.19.6 Employees who perform work while on a scaffold shall be trained by a qualified person to recognize the hazards associated with the type of scaffold being used, the nature of any electrical hazards, fall hazards, and falling object hazards in the work area. 5.19.7 Any scaffold damaged or weakened from any cause shall be immediately repaired or replaced and shall not be used until repairs have been completed. 5.19.8 Scaffolds shall not be loaded in excess of the working load for which they are intended. Safety Handbook For reference only. Invalid if printed. Page 36 of 39 5.19.9 Tools, materials, and debris shall not be allowed to accumulate in quantities to cause a hazard when working on a scaffold. 5.19.10 All scaffold planking must be approved and identified as scaffold grade. 5.19.11 Access to a scaffold shall be by secured ladder, or an equivalent safe access shall be provided. Climbing the side of scaffolding is not permitted. 5.19.12 Scaffolding greater than four feet in height must be equipped with handrails, mid- rails, toe boards, and be tightly planked. 5.19.13 Fall protection equipment including a full fall arrest system and retractable lanyard shall be worn and connected to an approved anchorage point or lifeline when working on any scaffold platform greater than four feet in height and not equipped with standard top rails and mid-rails or is not tagged 5.19.14 A scaffold tag signed by a competent person is required prior to allowing personnel to work on scaffolds. Check blocking to make sure that removing material will not result in a spill or shifting in other parts of the pile. 5.20.2 Avoid overloading shelves and overhead storage areas. Never store materials on shelves, roofs, or cabinets unless they are rated, and load posted.  In operating areas shelves, cabinets, lockers, toolboxes, etc. must be secured to prevent tip-over. 5.20.3 Storage capacity must be marked on all shelving designed for industrial storage. 5.20.4 Items in storage that weigh 50 pounds or more should be secured to a pallet and accessible to a forklift or other mechanical means for safe handling and storage. 5.20.5 Employees are not permitted to climb on piled sheets, slabs, scrap, coal, coke, plates, coils, pipe, or other material unless it is required by their job duties and documented in a Job Safety Procedure. 5.20.6 Loading & Unloading 5.20.7 Know the safe load limits and the approved methods of securing loads of piled materials. Never load any material handling equipment such as trailers, trucks, buggies, elevators, etc., beyond its safe limit. Tie or band material if necessary to prevent shifting. 1 Purpose/Scope          
1.1 This Energy Isolation Safety Standard outlines the responsibilities 
under this standard, minimum verification procedure, training, and 
periodic inspection requirements to protect people from potentially 
hazardous energy when servicing or performing maintenance on 
equipment, industrial vehicles, and machinery. 
1.2 When discussing hazardous energy, we mean any energy that can be 
released and might harm a person, such as: 
 
Chemical 
Temperature 
Gravity 
Motion 
Mechanical 
Electrical 
Pressure 
Sound 
Radiation  
Biological 
1.3 These are examples of hazardous energy being released and causing 
harm.  
 While workers are repairing a connection in piping, somewhere upstream of that 
repair, another worker opens a valve sending fluids down the pipe that spills on and 
burns the maintenance workers. 
 When a conveyor jams, a worker reaches in to try to clear the jam, when the jam is 
suddenly and unexpectedly freed, the worker is crushed as a result. 
 While a worker is servicing a machine, the internal wiring in the machine shorts, which 
causes the maintenance worker to be shocked. 
1.4 Energy Isolation ensures these types of hazardous energy sources are 
isolated, controlled, or rendered in a zero-energy state to perform 
servicing or maintenance safely. 
1.5 This Energy Isolation Safety Standard applies to all Cleveland-Cliffs 
Steel employees, contractors, sub-contractors, service providers, 
vendors, and visitors when: 
 Performing servicing and maintenance on equipment, industrial vehicles, or machines 
in which the energization or startup of the machines or equipment, or the release of 
stored energy, could harm employees regardless of the length of the exposure. 
 


--- SOURCE PDF PAGE 3 ---
Energy Isolation Safety Standard   
 
For reference only.   Invalid if printed.  
Page 3 of 52 
 Servicing and maintenance require the removal of machine guards or bypassing other 
safety devices. 
 Servicing and maintenance require personnel to place any part of their body into a 
point of operation, an area on a machine, a piece of equipment where work is 
performed, or into the danger zone associated with the machine's operation. 
1.6 This Energy Isolation Safety Standard does NOT apply to: 
 Work on cord and plug connected electrical equipment if the equipment is unplugged 
from the energy source, and the authorized employee has exclusive control of the 
plug. 
 Hot tapping operations. 
 Energized electrical work for purposes of diagnostic work. 
 Minor tool changes and adjustments and other minor servicing activities during 
normal production operations. 
 
 
 
 
  

--- SOURCE PDF PAGE 4 ---
Energy Isolation Safety Standard   
 
For reference only.   Invalid if printed.  
Page 4 of 52 
2 Responsibilities and Authorities 
2.1 This standard was jointly developed with participation from the 
represented workforce and management. 
2.2 Cleveland-Cliffs Steel is responsible for: 
 Providing this This Energy Isolation Safety Standard. 
 Complying with the various provisions of Federal, State, and Local rules and 
regulations. 
2.3 Plant General and Health and Safety Managers are responsible for: 
 Establishing and maintaining guidance and implementation documents in compliance 
with this Standard. 
 Implementing the safety inspection process for new or modified equipment. 
 Audit for compliance with this Standard. 
 Ensuring lockout/tryout initial, annual and refresher training are available and 
conducted in compliance with this Standard. 
 Investigating all lockout/tryout near misses, incidents, and injuries. 
2.4 Division Managers are responsible for: 
 Ensuring that Section and Shift Managers are trained on all aspects of this Energy 
Isolation Standard. 
 Ensuring employees attend energy Isolation training. 
 Investigating all lockout/tryout near misses, incidents, and injuries. 
 Ensuring that each energy isolation verification procedure receives a periodic 
inspection annually. 
2.5 Section Managers (Operations and Maintenance) are responsible for:  
 Ensuring correct lockout devices are available to control hazardous energy 
successfully. 
 Ensuring that the energy isolation verification procedures are developed and 
maintained for jobs/tasks in their area of responsibility. 
 Authorizing new or changed energy isolation verification procedures and compliance 
with this Standard. 
 Ensuring new or transferred employees receive hands-on training. 
 Ensuring employees attend energy isolation training. 
 Investigating all lockout/tryout near misses, incidents, and injuries. 
 
 


--- SOURCE PDF PAGE 5 ---
Energy Isolation Safety Standard   
 
For reference only.   Invalid if printed.  
Page 5 of 52 
2.6 Shift Managers (Operations and Maintenance) are responsible for:  
 Ensuring employees are trained on applicable energy isolation and verification 
procedures. 
 Shift Managers authorize group lockout leaders utilizing the energy isolation 
Authorized Employee Evaluation Form (CCS-HSS-FRM-0003.0). 
 Ensuring group and individual lockouts are performed when required. 
 Investigating all lockout/tryout near misses, incidents, and injuries. 
 Ensuring that employees, contract personnel, and visitors comply with the 
requirements detailed in this Standard. 
2.7 Employees are responsible for:  
 Reviewing and following energy isolation and verification procedures. 
 Signing on to a group lockout box control list. 
 Applying your personal safety lock to energy isolation devices, hasp, or a group 
lockout box. 
 Personal safety lock removal when appropriate. 
 Informing your manager if you have a concern with an energy isolation activity. 
 Compliance with the use of three-part communications. 
 Compliance with this Standard.  
2.8 A Group Lockout Leader is: 
 Experienced and knowledgeable of the machine/equipment operation. 
 Capable of recognizing hazardous energy sources, the type and magnitude of the 
energy available, and the methods and means necessary for energy isolation. 
 An authorized employee selected by their Shift Manager who meets the Group 
Lockout Leader evaluation criteria outlined in Form CCS-HSS-FRM-0003.0. 
 The above evaluation is one and done unless a periodic inspection, observation, or 
interaction reveals deviations or inadequacies in the employee's knowledge of Group 
Lockout Leader duties. 
 Trained to initiate energy isolation activities. 
 Trained to apply locks to energy isolation devices, perform second-person verification 
and try out equipment, 
 Trained to apply the control lock for the group lockout box and monitor completion of 
the group lockout box control list, 
 Not a permanent position unless the department makes it a permanent position. 
 Responsible for assessing the equipment, facilitating the group energy isolation 
verification procedure, maintaining continuity throughout the energy isolation and 
activity, and ensuring safe re-energization of the machine or equipment. 
2.8.1 It is essential to understand that the same person cannot apply the locks to energy 
isolation devices and verify the locks - Second Person Verification is required! 
2.8.2 Managers are to follow the training and retraining outlined in this document. 
 
 

--- SOURCE PDF PAGE 6 ---
Energy Isolation Safety Standard   
 
For reference only.   Invalid if printed.  
Page 6 of 52 
2.9 A Second Person Verifier is: 
 Experienced and knowledgeable of the machine/equipment operation. 
 Capable of recognizing hazardous energy sources, the type and magnitude of the 
energy available, and the methods and means necessary for energy isolation. 
 An employee selected and trained by their Shift Manager, to perform the duties 
outlined in this document. 
 Managers are to follow the training and retraining outlined in this document. 
 Responsible for walking down each assigned energy isolation device required to be 
locked out according to the energy isolation verification procedure to assure 
equipment lock(s) were applied and secured to all identified energy isolation devices 
(Verify the Locks). 
 Not a permanent position unless the department makes it a permanent position. 
 Second Person Verification is required when multiple people, multiple energy 
sources, or group lockout boxes are used. 
 Lockout involving just one authorized individual for a single energy source requires a 
“Tryout” of the equipment but does not require second-person verification. 
2.9.1 It is essential to understand that the same person cannot apply the locks and verify the 
locks - Second Person Verification is required! 
2.10 A Tester/Tryout Person is: 
 Experienced and knowledgeable of the machine/equipment operation. 
 Capable of recognizing hazardous energy sources, the type and magnitude of the 
energy available, and the methods and means necessary for energy isolation. 
 An employee selected and trained by their Shift Manager to perform the duties 
outlined in this document.  
 Responsible for ensuring the area/equipment cleared of workers, the area cleared of 
tools/materials, machine guards reinstalled and secured, lockout device(s) removed, 
informs affected employees, operates equipment (Tries Out), and returns controls to 
the “off” or “neutral” position after the tryout. 
 Not a permanent position unless the department makes it permanent.  
2.11 Group Lockout Leaders, Second Person Verifiers, and Testers can 
be cross-trained.  
2.12 There shall be a master list maintained in each division of these 
authorized employees trained for group lockout leaders, second-
person verifiers, and testers. Use form (CCS-HSS-FRM-0004.0, 
energy isolation Training Log).  
 
 
 

--- SOURCE PDF PAGE 7 ---
Energy Isolation Safety Standard   
 
For reference only.   Invalid if printed.  
Page 7 of 52 
2.12.1 Three-person example: Employee A (Group Lockout Leader) applies the locks, and 
Employee B (Second Person Verifier) walks down the unit and verifies the locks. Then, 
Employee C (Tester) tries out the equipment. 
2.12.2 Two-person example: Employee A (Group Lockout Leader) applies the locks, and 
Employee B (Second Person Verifier) walks down the unit and verifies the locks. Then, 
Employee A (Group Lockout Leader) or Employee B (Second Person Verifier) tries out 
the equipment. 
2.13 Responsibility for Lock Placement and Lock Removal 
2.13.1 The employee placing a personal safety lock on the energy isolation device is 
responsible for removing that lock. If the service being performed on the equipment 
has not been completed at shift change, or if the employee is called off the job, that 
employee must remove their personal safety lock(s). The incoming individual 
continuing the work must ensure that all energy sources are secured and properly 
locked out. 
2.13.2 If it is necessary to cut off a personal safety lock that an employee or contract 
employee failed or forgot to remove, approval must come from the Division Manager. 
A Safety Lock Removal Incident Report Form must be completed. 
2.13.3 A reasonable effort shall be made to contact the employee and ensure they are not at 
the worksite. This effort shall consist of: 
 Making phone or radio contact. 
 Checking clock-out records and sign-in sheets. 
 Thoroughly inspect the entire area to ensure the employee is not present. 
 If necessary to cut the personal safety lock, the employee must be notified before 
returning to work. 
2.13.4 Each employee is responsible for placing their personal safety lock on the correct 
energy isolation device or group lockout box. 
2.13.5 The ultimate responsibility to recognize, lock, try and ensure all hazardous energy 
sources lie within each person who might be required to apply or abide by the 
provisions of this Standard. 
 
  

--- SOURCE PDF PAGE 8 ---
Energy Isolation Safety Standard   
 
For reference only.   Invalid if printed.  
Page 8 of 52 
3 References and Definitions 
3.1 References 
 29 CFR 1910.147 OSHA (Occupational Safety & Health Administration) Lockout 
Standard 
 ANSI (American National Standards Institute) Z244.1-2016, the Control of Hazardous 
Energy Lockout and Alternative Controls 
3.2 Definitions 
 
Alternative Controls (under the minor tool changes, adjustments, and minor servicing 
exemption): The means of controlling hazardous energy (other than energy isolation) to reduce 
risk to an acceptable level. 
 Alternative controls may include devices such as but are not limited to engineered 
systems such as light curtains, pressure mats, area scanners, hold-to-run devices, 
interlock switches, stop devices, trapped key devices, specially designed tools, 
remote devices, interlocked barrier guards, local disconnects or keyed control 
switches, restraint devices that prevent the employee from entering the zone of 
danger, and Plexiglas or other physical and substantial protective barriers in a fixed 
position preventing the employee's body from entering the machine hazard area and 
adjacent equipment that could cause harm. 
 Before energy isolation is implemented on a unit, all alternative control devices shall 
be checked and verified that the control keys, switches, or interlocks are in their 
proper position and the unit is in normal operations mode. This ensures that no 
alternative controls interrupt normal operation and do not interfere with the energy 
isolation and verification. 
Authorized Employee: An employee who locks out machines or equipment to perform 
servicing or maintenance. 
Affected Employee: An employee who is required to use machines or equipment on which 
servicing or maintenance is being performed under the energy isolation standard or who 
performs other job responsibilities in an area where such servicing or maintenance is 
performed. An affected employee becomes an authorized employee when that employee's 
duties include servicing or maintenance. 
Blind: Is the absolute closure of a pipe, line, or duct achieved by fastening a solid plate, 
threaded plug, or cap across its bore to cover it completely. The cover must:  
A.  At least cover the outer edge of a flange’s mating surface. 
B.  Be capable of withstanding the maximum upstream system pressure during normal 
operations.  
C.  Blinds include blanks, slip plates, blind flanges, threaded caps, and physical 
disconnects. 
 The three types of blinds utilized include: 
 
A.  Isolation 
B.  Hydrotest 
C.  Permanent Blinds must be capable of holding the maximum pressure and 
temperature to which the blind will be exposed. 

--- SOURCE PDF PAGE 9 ---
Energy Isolation Safety Standard   
 
For reference only.   Invalid if printed.  
Page 9 of 52 
 Examples of acceptable handles are the “Spectacle,” "T handle,” or "J handle" design. 
 To eliminate the possibility of confusing restriction orifices with blinds, blinds with straight 
tabs must not be used. 
 
Figure 1 (above) - Blind-Flange Lockout Device 
 
 The crew securing the pipeline locks out upstream valves and then places a blank or 
blind in the system to positively block any potential downstream flow. 
 The flange bolts are then torqued to proper specification. At least one torqued bolt is 
covered with the blind-flange lockout device (see Figure 1 above). 
 The device is secured with one or more personal safety locks, or a group lockbox could 
be used. Multiple bolts could be covered using multiple devices if desired. 
Capable of Being Locked Out: An energy-isolating device is considered capable of being 
locked out if: 
 It is designed with a hasp or other means of attachment to which a lock can be affixed. 
 It has a locking mechanism built into it. 
 It can be locked without dismantling, rebuilding, replacing the energy-isolating device,

5.7 Seven Steps to Safe Equipment Shutdown 
 The following procedure shall be utilized to lockout and try out hazardous energy sources 
to achieve a zero-energy state when performing servicing and maintenance so that 
maintenance and servicing can be performed safely. 
5.7.1 Hazardous Energy Assessment – Before beginning work on equipment, perform a 
TAKE 5 to assess the equipment to determine the energy sources and the appropriate 
energy isolating devices. 
 Assess potentially hazardous stored or residual energy and initiate measures to relieve, 
disconnect, restrain or otherwise render “safe” any stored or residual energy. Ensure re-
accumulation of stored energy is not possible. 
 Consult the applicable energy isolation verification procedure. 
5.7.2 Notification – Notify all affected employees that an energy isolation procedure will be 
utilized. Do not proceed with the lockout until authorized by the equipment operator(s). 
5.7.3 Shutdown – Shut down or turn off the machine or equipment using normal or 
emergency shutdown procedures established for the machine or equipment. 
5.7.4 Isolate – Physically locate and isolate all energy isolating devices needed to control 
the energy to the machine or the equipment. 
5.7.5 Lockout – Authorized employees shall place and secure applicable lockout devices to 
each energy-isolating device identified in the energy isolation and verification 
procedure. Place your personal safety lock on the lockout device(s), locking them in a 
"safe" or zero energy position. In the case of a group lockout, place your personal 
safety lock on the group lockout box.
